Putting sensitive data into the URL isn't ideal, because there's a high risk of leaking it, e.g., through the Referer header. Additionally, URLs are often logged by the webserver and may be stored in an unsafe location for an indefinite duration.
So it's strongly recommended to put secrets into the request body or a header. If this isn't possible, you should at least disable the Referer header and be very careful about what gets logged where.

This depends on the properties of the token. If the token is instead valid for a long time and allows repeated logins then the risk can be significant - see the answer from Ja1024 for this.

I believe this is a misunderstanding. It's true that a website cannot change the hostname in the Origin header with client-side code. This also applies to cross-site scripting attacks. At best, the website or an XSS attacker can set the value to null by making the request from an opaque origin.
However, in the question you've linked to, it's a different scenario: The OP runs their own website, and now they want to reliably detect the origin of requests, even if the client misbehaves. In this case, the Origin header is useless, because the client can set it to anything they want. For example, they can use Burp Suite to alter the request headers, patch the browser code, use an alternative HTTP(S) client that allows setting the headers, change the outgoing HTTP(S) traffic etc.
So the comment is specifically about clients being able to manipulate the Origin header, not websites.

I was under the assumption that the browser sets this to the origin of the domain the request originates from, and that this cannot be influenced by the website that performs the request. Is that correct?

No. With respect to the first part, it is not safe to assume even that the client is a browser, much less that it behaves in any particular way.  Unjustified assumptions are a breeding ground for bugs and vulnerabilities.
Furthermore, an entity operating as a website does not, in that capacity, perform web requests.  It serves responses to web requests.  Web pages it serves may script requests back to it or to another site, but such scripting is a way to induce the client to make requests.  It does not constitute the website making them.  That is important because client behavior can be controlled on the client side to whatever extent the operator of the client desires.
Additionally, even if we assume that the client is not intentionally adversarial -- not at all a safe assumption -- software does have bugs. A standard-conforming EcmaScript implementation will not allow the Origin header to be manipulated programmatically, but it is not safe to assume that client-side script can't manipulate the Origin header just because it shouldn't be able to do.  Maybe the next big exploit will involve leveraging a bug in someone's ES implementation that allows client-side script to manipulate the Origin header after all.

The previous answers do a great job of answering the direct question you asked, so this is just to add a little context. The Origin HTTP header was created for a specific purpose, CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), which is a standardized protocol by which script running in a browser can make requests to origins other than that of the page it's currently executing on, and the server at that other origin can deliberately create a hole in the same-origin policy (SOP) that normally prevents one origin from accessing responses (and some other kinds of content) from another origin. Origin is the request (client-set) header that tells the other origin's server where the request originated.
SOP is extremely important to browser security. It's the thing that makes it safe to do online banking and business and social media and anything else that requires logging in, even while you have other sites open, without worrying that a malicious script will read the data from the logged-in site (including anti-CSRF tokens that would allow the malicious script to successfully make authenticated requests to make changes on the other site). Weakening it, as CORS does, should only be used for sites with no sensitive data (e.g. totally public sites), or where the other site trusts the requesting origin. As such, browsers don't allow scripts to set the Origin header, or else a malicious site A could serve your browser a script that sends CORS requests to CORS-using site B, and B doesn't trust A but the script spoofs the requests as coming from origin C that is trusted by B. This would have the effect of mostly turning off SOP for all CORS-enabled sites.
However, SOP is a browser security feature. It is built around some assumptions that apply to browsers, and not to most other kinds of apps:

The client is potentially authenticated to one site while interacting with another.
The client automatically attaches certain kinds of authentication credentials (such as HTTP Authorization: Basic or Digest passwords, or Kerberos tickets, or HTTPS client certificates, or - most commonly - cookies) to requests, without the requester needing to know the credential.
The client downloads and executes scripts and other content from potentially-untrustworthy sites.
The client can make requests to other origins on behalf of downloaded scripts or other content.
The client sandboxes downloaded scripts such that even malicious ones cannot, for example, simply make unrestricted web requests.

When operating outside of those conditions, SOP doesn't usually apply. Many apps have embedded web browser components, and those generally try to follow SOP, but even then they don't necessarily comply; for example, such an app might expose to JavaScript a function that makes web requests directly without going through the browser component's XHR/Fetch APIs (and thereby bypasses SOP). Tons of other apps - including obvious ones like curl or even just raw connections via netcat or similar - allow completely unrestricted web requests with arbitrary header values. This is why you can't rely on the Origin header to tell you authoritatively where a request comes from!
The purpose of the Origin header is to tell the server "assuming that I am a browser making this request on behalf of a client-side script, this is where the script is executing" and ask it "do you want to allow the originating script - again, assuming there is one - to make the request (pre-flight only) / see the response ('simple' CORS requests that don't get a pre-flight)?" Outside of this intended use case, it's just another string, potentially useful in an advisory context but you shouldn't make security decisions on the basis of it alone.
As a side note, the use of Origin for purposes other than CORS requests - it is now sent for all non-GET, non-HEAD requests, even same-origin or submitted by HTML <form> or sent using fetch in non-CORS mode - is a later extension to the specification. I believe all modern browsers adhere to this behavior, but older ones - such as on outdated mobile devices, or anywhere Internet Explorer is still used, for example - might not, even if they otherwise adhere to the CORS specification (including use of Origin for CORS requests). Thus, with modern browsers you can extend the trusted use cases to also include "assuming that I am a browser making this request on behalf of client-side content, this is the origin in which that content is loaded". However, even if you expect your users to only run current browsers, that doesn't tell you anything about somebody making requests from a mobile app or through a Python script. Thus you should only use it to make security decisions such that, if the requesting agent is not a browser, the outcome of the security decision doesn't matter.
Compartmentalisation: "The client sandboxes downloaded scripts such that even malicious ones cannot, for example, simply make unrestricted web requests." The mention of sandboxing as a containment strategy is an explicit reference to the idea of isolating security risks. Compartmentalisation is about segregating resources to limit exposure and impact, which is exactly what sandboxing does.
Minimum trust and maximum trustworthines: You can't rely on the Origin header to tell you authoritatively where a request comes from! This is an explicit statement about not trusting an external input (the Origin header) as a reliable security mechanism. The principle of Minimum Trust emphasises that systems should not assume external components are trustworthy and should instead verify inputs and behaviors. The warning not to base security decisions on the Origin header alone is a direct application of this principle.

If a deterministic CPU instruction misbehaves, this is at least in principle detectable through incorrect results, be it in real-world applications or systematic tests.
This doesn't apply to RDRAND, because there is no ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?correct?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂª?ÃÂ result. Of course you can run statistical tests to detect obvious flaws, but this doesn't prevent backdoors. For example, pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) can be entirely deterministic and still pass all kinds of statistical tests. If RDRAND uses such a PRNG, somebody who knows the seed might be able to reconstruct all past values or predict future values, which is obviously a problem if the numbers are used for sensitive purposes like generating keys or nonces.

In addition to the answer from Ja1024:
Backdooring RNG is a real threat, as can be seen by  DUAL EC DRBG. This PRNG was backdoored by the RSA and was shipped in critical production software (SDK from RSA) and systems (Juniper VPN). In the last case it meant that an attacker could passively sniff the encrypted VPN traffic but could decrypt it with the knowledge of the secret backdoor.
Note that (presumably) neither RSA nor Juniper were aware of the backdoor, they just implemented an algorithm which was standardized by NIST. And this could happen with CPU vendors too which implement an RNG officially deemed to be secure.
It is also not possible to detect such a backdoor just by looking at the output. The output still looks random and passes statistical tests. It is also not predictable, except when one has knowledge of the specific backdoor.
And even if the random generator is not backdoored it might still have weaknesses which are not obvious at first. See this wikipedia entry for prominent examples of such failures and their critical impact.
It is therefore common practice and not unique to Linux to rely on multiple independent sources for randomness.

In the case of a random number generator: You might have received source code that you compile and run in a sandbox. The code cannot possibly attack your computer in any way.
Now you use the random number generator to produce private RSA keys. But the attacker has given you a fake random number generator that produces predictable random numbers, and as a result your computer produces private RSA keys that are predictable. So even though your computer is completely safe it can produce data that puts you (not your computer) at risk.
Or say you run Monte Carlo simulations to help you decide if you should make a certain investment. A random number generator under control of an attacker might change your simulations in a way that make a bad investment look like a good one.

DISCLAIMER: I will answer from a strictly security perspective. But, we should keep in mind that security comes at the expanse of usability. And in any real environment, the security measures applied should take into consideration the real security risks the environment is exposed to and the operational needs.
Secure the service or the resource first
The first thing to take care of is to not expose an application to unneeded remote hosts or networks.
Most of the software you mentioned can be configured to only listen on the loopback interface, or to only listen on the interface you need.
More specifically on Kurbenetes and Docker solutions:
You don't have to expose the containers to all interfaces if they are not supposed to. Those solutions can manage their own internal network infrastructure. You can configure a container to be only accessible by another container on their on virtual private network if you want ti. Be aware that most default (no-brainer copy-paste) tutorial will not follow the recommended security practices and will makes everything opens for conveniences.
Always use a firewall
Unless one knows why they don't need to enable a firewall, ALWAYS enable and configure the firewall. Even if there is no services or resources listening on a network socket.
Then any incoming traffic shall be denied or rejected by default to only allow explicitly the incoming traffic needed. The list of what is needed by default might require some network computing knowledge and understanding of the environment but the most basic things are:

Allow incoming traffic on the loopback interface
Allow incoming traffic that matches outcoming traffic initiated by the host (like a response to a web request made on the web browser of the host). This traffic is referred to on the Linux kernel packet filtering solution as traffic with the state RELATED or ESTABLISHED.
Allow some ICMPv6 traffic for IPv6 to be configured and to work properly on the host.

How to use UFW the most simple way?
UFW (which is the default front-end on Ubuntu to the Linux kernel packet filter) makes thing simple. Doing a ufw enable will configure the firewall with the default configuration defined in /etc/default/ufw. So by default, ufw enable will do the following actions (among others):

DROP all incoming packets except for:

those destined to the loopback interface
those matching prior outgoing traffic you initiated
Some ICMP and ICMPv6 traffic (which allows your computer to receive and respond to ICMP ping, and do all basic networking stuff with IPv6).
DHCP traffic
mDNS and SSDP traffic
User defined rules


ALLOW outgoing packets
DROP forwarded packets (packets not destined to the host and that would required to be routed)

Then, the user can add its own rules to allow specific network traffic.
NOTE: In the case one needs another remote host to connect to a specific service or resource on the host. It is NOT a security good practice to allow the whole network subnet of the remote host to access the host blindly. One should only allow this specific host (through IP address filtering for example) to connect to the specific service or resource (through protocol and port filtering for example).
Minimum exposure: The comment explicitly states: "The first thing to take care of is to not expose an application to unneeded remote hosts or networks." This is a direct explanation of the principle, emphasizing that unnecessary exposure should be avoided.
Secure fail-safe defaults: "Then any incoming traffic shall be denied or rejected by default to only allow explicitly the incoming traffic needed." This directly explains the principle of default deny security.

There are standards for individual aspects of what you you want to do, but I'm not aware of a single standard which specifies an entire web application for storing encrypted data.
It is possible to securely derive multiple secrets from the same password, or to use the the password both for authentication and encryption. However, the approach you've chosen isn't secure. Using a general-purpose hash algorithm instead of a specialized password hashing function like Argon2 is a very bad idea, because it makes the hash highly susceptible to brute-force attacks. Based on your description, you do expose pass_hash1 to the server, so if that server is malicious or compromised, it can attack the password. This should also answer your third question.
One approach to use a password for multiple purposes is to first run it through a specialized password hashing function like Argon2 and then a key derivation function like HKDF. The first protects the password from brute-force attacks, the second allows you to derive one or more arbitrarily long secrets from the password hash. Alternatively, since Argon2 in particular can also be used as a password-based key derivation function, you could just generate a single output which is sufficiently long to split it into a password hash for authentication and an encryption key:
# desired length (in bytes) of the password hashes
password_hash_length = 32
# desired length (in bytes) of the encryption key
key_length = 32

derived_secret = argon2(
  password: user_password, 
  output_length: password_hash_length + key_length
)
password_hash = derived_secret.substring(
  start: 0, 
  length: password_hash_length
)
key = derived_secret.substring(
  start: password_hash_length, 
  length: key_length
)

If you want to make sure the hash is deterministic and doesn't change with every call, you have to store the hash parameters (algorithm version, salt, number of iterations etc.). When you hash the password with the exact same parameters, you get the exact same hash.
However, the whole procedure still seems rather awkward. How about this:

The client encrypts a file on their own machine. Ideally, this would happen outside of the browser or at least not with JavaScript, because a malicious or compromised server could easily sabotage any JavaScript-based encryption procedure, and there's no realistic way for a user to recognize and prevent this. It's up to the client to generate the key randomly (which is preferable) or derive it from a password. In the latter case, it's crucial to use a password-based key derivation function like Argon2.
Additionally, the client generates a random ID and submits both the ID and the ciphertext to the server.
The server hashes the ID (SHA-2 is enough) and stores the ciphertext under the ID hash. It's possible to additionally encrypt the ciphertext server-side to provide some protection even if the user-chosen key is weak.
Whenever the client wants to retrieve their data, they provide the ID, get back the ciphertext from the server and can then decrypt the ciphertext.

This should achieve all your goals while being both more secure and simpler:

The server (or any attacker who has compromised the server) never sees any hash based on the password. At best, they could try to brute-force a password-based key using the ciphertext, but as long as both the password and the key derivation function are reasonable strong, this should be infeasible.
As there are no user accounts, it's not possible to associate any ciphertext with any user based on the stored data alone. Of course this doesn't provide full anonymity, because a malicious or compromised server could try browser fingerprinting or a traffic analysis.
Clients cannot obtain a ciphertext without knowing the random identifier.
It's infeasible to reconstruct the identifiers from the stored hashes, so even if an attacker manages to obtain hashes, they cannot get the corresponding ciphertext through the web application.
If the ciphertexts are encrypted server-side, then it's also not possible to get them from server storage without first obtaining the server key.

There's a theoretical and a practical answer.
In theory, you could audit the entire client code and make sure that it implements an end-to-end encryption protocol where the messages cannot be decrypted except by the chat participants. This is how TLS works, for example: No matter how many intermediate hosts the traffic flows through, none of them can get the plaintext (leaving aside bugs, misconfigurations or cryptographic weaknesses). You could even write your own Telegram client from scratch.
In practice, very few people will actually read the entire source code and then ensure that the app they have on their device has actually been built from this exact code. This leaves plently of room for backdoors, undocumented behavior or honest mistakes.
So realistically, there's very little we as average users can say with confidence, let alone ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?prove?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂª?ÃÂ. We can read the design documents, maybe do a basic check of the code, maybe analyze the traffic, but that's pretty much it. A researcher or auditor who is willing to spend a lot of time on the code can certainly do more, even prove some properties with a mathematical model of the protocol. But even that doesn't give any guarantees. Just look how many vulnerabilities have been found in TLS despite it being a completely open, widely used and very mature protocol.

Given the goal, since the account had MFA, then it is reasonable to assume that all current access is legitimate and authorised. Expiring current sessions does not appear to have a security goal when lowering security controls.

It is very reasonable - and, indeed, standard practice - to require that the user re-authenticate when they request to disable MFA (or otherwise change the login process, especially in a way that could make it easier). This both protects against attackers with temporary session access but no credentials being able to establish ongoing control, and (if implemented correctly, which is a significant "if") is a very strong protection against common web attacks such as XSS, CSRF, clickjacking, etc. being used to make the user's account more vulnerable.
Given that you require re-authentication when the change is made, it's not necessary to terminate all sessions after removing MFA. If the change was made by an attacker, that attacker has just proven themselves to be able to authenticate even while MFA was enabled in which case that account is already totally compromised and ending sessions would do basically nothing. If the change was legitimate, there's no need to inflict a bad user experience on the user.
To be clear, it's also a good idea to send out a notification (e.g. via email, SMS, and/or within the site/app if you have a built-in notification channel) when security settings are changed. Don't leave the user in the dark! And sure, signing them out unexpectedly is sort of like notifying them that something has happened. Unfortunately, it doesn't really work for that purpose. Generally, the user will just assume your site sucks and re-enter their credentials, same as they do all the time on lots of other sites that require unnecessarily frequent re-authentication. You could use the login page specifically to display an alert explaining why they got logged out - the changed to the MFA setting - and maybe they'd read that, but I wouldn't really expect that to be much more effective than either an in-app, in-session notification, or an out-of-app (e.g. email) notification, and I don't think it warrants the bad UX.

(The rest of this answer isn't really about your question directly, though it is related to why you shouldn't log users out when there's no real security benefit, aside from the cost to UX.)
A point about the danger of unnecessary or poorly-designed login UX: it's corrosive to users' abilities to make good security decisions. Consider the following scenarios:

I follow a link to a site that I expect to be logged into, but am greeted with a login page instead. If the site is reliable about remembering my authentication status, I'm going to be much more suspicious - of phishing, mostly - than if the site expires my session twice a month without warning or action on my part.
I'm trying to log into a site, but it's not accepting my password. Maybe I forgot it, maybe the password I signed up with is too long for the login form to accept (a scenario that shouldn't happen but I've seen multiple times!), maybe somebody is trying to brute-force my password and the site has locked my account. If I do the password reset flow, supply a new password, and it succeeds... log me in! If you bounce me back to the login page again, then whatever problem I was having before will likely happen again, and even if it doesn't, you haven't gained any security by doing so. However, if it does happen again, I'm likely to start using weaker passwords - shorter, more limited character space, etc. - that will make it both more likely that I forget again in future (because it's a worse password than I'd normally use) and increase the risk that my account is breached.
While interacting with a site that doesn't seem obviously untrustworthy, but doesn't have a strong established reputation, I'm invited to link my bank account (maybe it's a site for tracking my expenses, or making charitable donations without credit card fees, or whatever). The site then mocks up my bank's login page, and tells me to enter the bank login credentials (yeah I'm not even vagueing, this is about the atrocity that is Plaid). If I follow good security practice and never give my credentials to any third-party app/site, I can't use this. If I decide that yeah, OK, it's probably fine... well, best case, they handle them as-responsibly-as-possible-given-the-premise, and all I really have to worry about is either that company getting breached, or me in future becoming complacent and entering them on a site that isn't even quasi-respectable and is phishing for Plaid users. Which is of course the worst-case scenario, the best defense against which is the entirely reasonable policy "never give your creds for X to third party Y". (Some caveat for password managers, but you want to be very careful about their trustworthiness, make sure they use zero-knowledge end-to-end encryption, and you shouldn't ever enter your password manager's master password on any website.)
On a site's login page, I find that due to some stupid JS+CSS tricks (autocomplete=false isn't sufficient, browsers are explicitly required to ignore that for password fields), my password manager won't auto-fill it, and I can't paste the password either. This means I can't realistically use a strong password - one that's long, really random, etc. - so I'll choose a much weaker one, easy enough to confidently remember and not too annoying to type.
Usability: The comment explicitly explains how poor login UX weakens security by encouraging insecure behaviors like password reuse, phishing susceptibility, and frustration-driven mistakes.

So I basically need to verify that some-website.com is making the request and not anyone else by verifying the domain. Is this problem even solvable?

It is possible to limit requests made by the browser in this way, for example by checking the Origin header. However, people can still make requests outside of a browser (e.g. with curl or Burp), and then there is no way for you to tell whether it is a legitimate request or not.

If the server of some-website.example.com made the request to gptproxy.example.com, then the latter could easily identify the server based on authentication or IP address. However, you wrote that some-website.example.com is a frontend-only site, which means the requests are actually sent by the users of some-website.example.com.
In this case, some-website.example.com must provide its users with (ideally short-lived) authorization tokens which are included in all requests to gptproxy.example.com and can be verified by the proxy. As an example approach:

some-website.example.com generates a key pair, registers at gptproxy.example.com and provides its public key. This key is stored on the gptproxy.example.com server and associated with gptproxy.example.com.
When a user visits some-website.example.com, the server generates a JSON Web Token (JWT) and wraps it in a JSON Web Signature (JWS). The server uses the JWT for authorization data (e.g., that the user is permitted to make requests to the proxy within a certain timeframe) and signs this data with its private key. The resulting JWS is embedded into the response page, so that it's automatically included in all subsequent requests to gptproxy.example.com.
When gptproxy.example.com receives a request with an included JWS, it can verify the signature with the stored public key and read the JWT to check whether the user is authorized to use one of the API keys.

Note that in the above scheme, the actual request data is not covered by the signature, so the user can set it to anything they want. Also note that if some-website.example.com doesn't have user authentication, it's very easy for a third party to constantly request new tokens from some-website.example.com and use them for accessing gptproxy.example.com. However, this would be a problem of some-website.example.com which needs to be fixed on their end.
From a security perspective, the idea of having gptproxy.example.com collect the API keys of all  isn't great either. You should double-check if there are alternatives which make use of short-lived credentials (e.g., the OAuth protocol).

You don't authenticate the payload, you only authenticate the random number this way. A man in the middle attacker might change the payload while keeping the random number the same.
Instead of choosing a random number for protection which is independent from the payload you need to derive the protection from the payload in order to detect modifications to the payload. HMAC is a suitable algorithm for this. In this case one also only needs to transport once the secret for all the HMACs out of band.

As described, the connection would be secure. However, "the physical security of this cable is okay" is doing a lot of work; for example, can an attacker get close enough to pick up the electrical fields from transmissions on the wire? If so, you'd better (EDIT: thank you @user71659) use fiber-optic cables! You might also want to encrypt, though there's still a risk from traffic analysis. Additionally, saying neither host "supports routing from other interfaces" is kind of weird; all major operating systems allow configuring the route table - this is how VPNs and similar software work, they create a virtual network interface and set it as the default route - but accepting for the moment that premise, you're in pretty good shape, security-wise. If your direct connection really is secure enough, you can be sure that the other host is the only peer on the connection, which means you can forego authentication of the host, and potentially also encryption.
There are still some angles for attacking such a system from the hosts themselves. If the connection is ever not locked down such that a different process on one of the hosts can access it, they might be able to spoof outbound traffic or - depending on the protocol - potentially intercept inbound messages. Furthermore, even without the ability to edit the route table or install additional network interfaces, a sufficiently-privileged attacker can install a driver (or, in some cases, use a pre-installed network tap driver) to directly monitor the bits flowing through the network stack (this is how Wireshark and similar programs work). Of course, a sufficiently-privileged attacker can also just attach to the software on their host like a debugger, giving the ability to read and modify all process memory including the incoming and outgoing network traffic. Situations where an attacker can tap the network traffic but not inspect the process memory directly are possible, but scarce.

Security is seldom an absolute concept. You implement protections to avoid some kind of attacks, and try to reach an optimum between security and usability. Do not forget that the most secure system is a system set to off, with no connection (even to a power socket) and stored inside a physical safe. No possible direct attack vector. But kind of useless...
As you do not say what are the threats you want to considere, I cannot tell you if the system will resist them. The best I can do is tell you what attack vectors I can imagine in that context.

external and technically complex:
Electrical field analysis - even if it is very hard do interpret them, it is theorically possible to build side channel attacks through them

internal but technical:
The security of a network cannot be higher than the security of its nodes. If at any moment the security of one of the machines has been compromised, it can be used to attack the other one. Only you know whether it can be a real use case...

social

The reason for this requirement is explained in section 3.2.4 of the original SRP paper.
If B is sent before A, then an attacker who has managed to obtain the password verifier v = g^x of another user (e.g., through an SQL injection), can successfully authenticate as this user without knowing their password-derived secret x. This works by sending a crafted A which cancels out the x term in the calculations of the shared secret S.
All calculations are modulo N:

Contrary to the standard protocol, the server first sends B = v + g^b to the attacker who masquerades as a legitimate client.
Knowing both v and B, the attacker can craft A as A = g^a * v^(-u), where u are the first 32 bits of SHA1(B). This A is what the attacker sends to the server.
According to the protocol, the server calculates the shared secret as S = (A * v^u)^b, which in this case results in S = (g^a * v^(-u) * v^u)^b = g^(ab). Note that the verifier v = g^x and therefore the secret x have been completely cancelled out due to the choice of A.
The attacker can calculate this shared secret with S = (B - v)^a = (v + g^b - v)^a = g^(ab).
Now the attacker is able to prove they know the session key K = SHA_Interleave(S).

This attack only works because the attacker knows B (and with it u) before they have to send their A. If the server follows the standard and demands A before revealing B, there's no way for the attacker to craft their A based on knowledge of B.
On a side note: SRP has been revised several times, and RFC 2945 describes the old version 3. The current version 6a is described in RFC 5054 in the context of TLS (it's referred to as version 6 in the RFC, but this is an error).

Once you allowed the browser to reach the site by HTTPS though, the client got both a 301 permanent redirect and a HSTS policy (HTTP header Strict-Transport-Security) from the server. To be more specific:

www.williamhill.es then has the STS header

and that www.williamhill.es should only be visited by HTTPS due to the HSTS policy.

Important disclaimer: it's been a long time since I was looking into searchable encryption, and I'm not well-informed on the topic. Don't count on my understanding here; it's likely I've missed some things in this answer.
Searchable encryption is hard, and you're asking for a lot. As of Jan 2025, I'm not aware of any published library that can achieve this. It might1 be technically possible to do this securely - meaning, it achieves all your goals while the security of the encryption is weakened by no more than the degree inherent in the attacker knowing that the plaintext is constrained to values which match the validation rules - but the compute costs could rapidly become enormous, especially with large messages and/or variable-length regexes.
Searchable encryption approaches do exist, and more advanced ones are an area of active research. However, they tend to have serious limitations in confidentiality (exposing information about the ciphertext even if no specific byte range is necessarily decryptable), practicality (requiring excessive storage space or compute time), and/or applicability (usable only with restricted search queries, messages that match certain common structures, or similar). Regexes in particular are hard. Searchable encryption can also sometimes run into the problem of only getting "fuzzy" matching, which can result in false positives (in your scenario, a valid input that incorrectly gets flagged as invalid).
In this answer, I'm going to be looking at the two approaches that @Ja1024 shared: a 2014 paper called "RESeED: A secure regular-expression search tool for storage clouds" by Salehi et al, and a 2017 paper titled "Pattern Matching on Encrypted Streams" by Desmoulins et al, which introduces "Searchable Encryption with Shiftable Trapdoors" or SEST. I'm not sure2 that either is fully capable of solving your need. However, even if not, SEST is remarkably close, and it may be in the future that some such searchable encryption algorithm is widely available.
RESeED proposes building on a familiar form of searchable encryption, "public key encryption with keyword search" or "PEKS", wherein strings you may want to search for are encrypted along with the message. RESeED introduces some elements to make the search more generic - allowing searching for keywords, and regular expressions whose tokens are such "keywords", that were not known at encryption time - without greatly bloating the storage space.
That's very impressive, but it contains some severe limitations. First, it uses a fuzzy match; the purpose of the algorithm is to support creating essentially a search index that allows the data owner to identify encrypted messages matching a particular search query (without revealing either the messages or the query to the storage provider), whereupon the owner downloads the identified messages and presumably decrypts them, searches them directly, and throws out any false positives. That's not the use case you're looking at here, and although efforts can be taken to reduce the risk of false positives, it comes at the cost of storage size and compute and only asymptotically approaches zero (though being close enough to zero is in fact good enough; that's the principle underlying e.g. all password hashing and digital signing based on secure hash functions). Second, it depends on an "alphabet division" whereby the symbols of the message are divided into "core" symbols that make up the searchable tokens, and "separator" symbols that delimit tokens. This is fine if (e.g.) your messages consist of English text; separators would be characters like punctuation and whitespace, while everything else (printable) would be core. Unfortunately, that means you can't really search on substrings of a token, and in particular doesn't really allow searching for a specific character (symbol) that appears embedded in various tokens (words); you would need to search for all possible tokens containing that symbol. Furthermore, while I'd need to do more reading to confirm this3, I suspect that the existence of the data structures involved here - which functionally implement an encrypted search index - leak data if an actor without the key is permitted to perform the searches; such an "attacker" could infer things about the tokens based on how many messages they appear in (using e.g. word frequency statistics) and thus about those messages themselves (especially if they can watch the structures update as new messages are added).
SEST is more promising. It focuses on a completely different use case, where the key holder and message transport provider (or "gateway") are in a cooperative but mutually untrusting relationship, and the gateway needs to inspect the encrypted traffic for various contents without decrypting it. This much more closely matches your use case. It's also far more focused on preserving the confidentiality of the messages. However, SEST still differs from your scenario somewhat: it proposes a separate sender and recipient, and uses public key cryptography rather than symmetric encryption; these may or may not pose a problem. SEST is also less focused on regular expressions, but in a way that's probably beneficial to your use case; it focuses on the ability to search out arbitrary patterns - including single symbols and wildcards - but this can be used to build regular expression matches too.
However, SEST also has limitations. It requires public keys linear in the size of the message, which is potentially very large. The ciphertext is also large, though again at least it is only linear in size of the message. The search process itself is expensive, especially for short "keywords" (queries, which can contain wildcards) in long messages; the optimizations that can be performed for plain-text matching aren't available. (On the other hand, it is at least highly parallelizable.) A potential further complication is that SEST is built using "trapdoors": search query values that are applied to the ciphertext in order to find matches, but which can only be created by the holder of the private key (recipient), and are not readily inspectable by the gateway. The gateway (who, like the sender, has the public key) is able to verify simple trapdoors by encrypting strings that should or should not match the trapdoor and testing them, but this requires using public key encryption rather than symmetric keys. It also is not clear to me that this is secure against a scenario wherein the recipient (user), hoping to sneak something past the gateway (storage service), creates a trapdoor that appears to match the gateway's requested query but doesn't reliably do so. It's easy - though somewhat computationally expensive - to test for that with simple search queries (like "contains the character 'x'"), but regexes are much harder. As an example, the difference between the regexes /foo.*bar/ and /foo[^~]*[^q]*[^&]*bar/ is quite hard to experimentally detect, in terms of what they'll match. A gateway (validator) that thinks it has a trapdoor for the former but actually has one for the latter will miss an attacker who intentionally embeds the characters ~, q, &, in that order, in between the forbidden foo...bar portions. Given how SEST works, and depending on the regexes that you're actually checking, that might not be a problem in practice (you can check for /foo.*bar/ by separately checking for foo and bar, which are "normal" search strings and thus relatively easy to validate trapdoors for, and comparing the indices at which they appear)... but it might also be a huge problem in practice. You'd also need to figure out a way to either convert your design to asymmetric cryptography, or wrap SEST within symmetric cryptography, without compromising the security of the design.
With all that said, the fact that there have been at least4 two papers on searchable encryption with regular expressions, one now over a decade old, is hopeful. You should definitely do some research and may want to come back with a more specific question,

First, because this is largely untested academic cryptography, and much likelier than established primitives and constructions to contain errors that weaken the security (and even if the design is secure, any given implementation may well not be, as they won't yet be extensively reviewed). Second, because the specific properties you are requesting don't exactly match any cipher I'm aware of, and trying to adapt an advanced cryptographic primitive to a different use case than intended is fraught indeed.
2 I am not a cryptographer, and my work with cryptography is generally confined to the application of well-known primitives and constructions to specific, but not especially novel, applications. This is well outside of that, and you should consider seeking those with greater expertise.
3 Specifically, I'd need to do a bunch of reading about PEKS, which I expect leaks considerable privacy when used with arbitrary, rather than specific predefined, tokens.

The signature is an ECDSA signature of the tag UID. Based on the proxmark3 source code, there are some variations of how the signature is calculated and represented: The signature may be calculated over the UID itself or a SHA-256 hash of the UID, and the signature bytes may or may not be stored in reverse order on the card. I don't know what that depends on (maybe the tag model), but proxmark3 tries all possible combinations, converts the input into an ASN.1 structure and uses the standard ECDSA signature calculations.
All public keys which proxmark3 uses for signature verification are hard-coded into the source code. You can also obtain them through NXP, and they might be stored on the tag according to section 8.2 of the datasheet. Note that signature verification only makes sense when you're sure the public key is correct. Anybody can create an ECDSA key pair and sign arbitrary data. To make sure the data has actually been signed by NXP, you need to verify the signature with their public key and not any other key.
This should also answer your third question: Yes, it's possible to put an arbitrary signature and public key onto a forged tag. What a counterfeiter cannot do is pass the verification check against a public key of NXP unless they a) clone an authentic UID/signature pair or b) obtain NXP's private key or c) manage to find some major cryptographic vulnerability. The impact of a successful attack (which will likely consist of duplicating a known UID) depends on what exactly the UID is used for in the target environment. For example, if this environment relies on the UID for authentication, then obtaining and duplicating a UID allows an attacker to impersonate somebody else.
As to troubleshooting steps: Obtain the correct public key (ideally through NXP directly) and check if it matches any of the hard-coded keys in the proxmark3 code. Find out which of the signature variations in the code NXP actually uses for the tag (if any) by looking this up in the datasheet or asking NXP. Then calculate the UID signature yourself with some ECC library (not proxmark3). Does the result match the proxmark3 result? Does it match the stored signature?

This GitHub repository is not the official repository of BearSSL (and I have no idea who put it there or why). The official repository is https://www.bearssl.org/git/BearSSL (that's the address you'd give to git; to browse the source code, use: https://bearssl.org/gitweb/?p=BearSSL;a=summary).
AES/GCM is supported in TLS, with the specific implementation being in the src/ssl/ssl_rec_gcm.c file. There is also a standalone AES/GCM API (if you want to use that outside of TLS), which is documented in inc/bearssl_aead.h. "AEAD" means Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data, i.e. not only encryption but also a check that the data was not modified, and that extra check also covers additional non-encrypted data. In the same header, you'll find that two other AEAD mode based on AES are implemented, EAX and CCM.

TPSPs do not automatically excuse you from all PCI Requirements
Just because PCI rules are easier to manage when using a Third Party Service Provider does not mean they all go away.  As an online vendor, PCI compliance is ultimately your responsibility.  PCI DSS only requires a TPSP like Stripe to be responsible for the parts of your PCI burden that they agree to take on in their service agreement with you. See PCI's Third-Party Security Assurance document for more details. In simple terms, this means that their responsibility for assuring your PCI compliance ends at your ability to follow the Terms of Service of your agreement with them, and any reputable TPSP like Stripe will require you to use HTTPS because there is no way for them to guarantee a secure transaction without it.
Stripe's current integration guide specifically requires you to use HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or above on any payment pages on your website.  So, if you use HTTP on a payment page with Stripe, Stripe will not assume the responsibility of PCI compliance on those transactions.  So not only does this mean that you are not PCI compliant, but it also means that you will be the party reasonable for negligence and damages if something bad comes of it.
The reason this is insecure, and a PCI violation, is because it allows a MITM attack to redirect traffic to a whole different website and payment system in which case you have literally none of the features of Stripe in place to protect yourself or your clients.  So even if you can "get away with" not having HTTPS on parts of your website under Stripe's ToS, you may still be sued for gross negligence if such an attack were ever done on one of your customers.
You should always use HTTPS, even when it is not "required"
Honestly, you really should encrypt every single website in its entirety with HTTPS because the end user only needs to arrive on one HTTP page for an MITM to alter some links and ship your user off to their Evil Twin version of your website. If they do that, your customers could still be fooled into making a fraudulent payment, giving up credentials, or downloading malware, even if your real site does not have any e-commerce features.

Section 2.1 introduces JWT bearer tokens as a new authorization grant for OAuth 2.0. This grant can be used instead of the four standard grants (like the Authorization Code Grant or the Client Credentials Grant) to request an access token from the authorization server. Note that the JWT bearer token doesn't contain the client credentials and may have to be combined with client authentication. For example, in the Microsoft On-Behalf-Of flow, the authorization server expects both a JWT bearer token as part of the grant and client credentials for authentication (either a shared secret or another JWT bearer token).
Section 2.2 defines how JWT bearer tokens can be used as a method for client authentication within a grant type like the Authorization Code Grant or the Client Credentials grant. For example, the client presents both an authorization code and a bearer token with the client credentials to satisfy the requirements from section 3.2.1 of RFC 6749: If a client has been issued credentials, it must present them to the authorization server when requesting an access token. If the Client Credentials Grant is used, then the credentials in the JWT bearer token are already sufficient to satisfy the grant requirements.
Both cases are unrelated and can even be combined: You can use JWT tokens both as a grant type and as a mechanism for user authentication, as pointed out in the second-to-last paragraph in the introduction.
To again point out the difference between the jwt-bearer grant and the Client Credentials Grant:

In the first case, the JWT bearer token holds some information (like an access token provided by another client) which authorizes the current client to obtain a new access token. If the authorization server additionally requires client authentication, then the client has to present separate client credentials, e.g., a shared secret or another JWT bearer token.
In the second case, the JWT bearer token itself contains the client credentials and therefore already satisfies the requirements of the Client Credentials Grant.

Client-Side Encryption Can Add an Extra Layer of Security
This is an absolute last line of defense kind of thing, but when working with systems that transfer money, it's generally a good idea.  If all of your other security attempts fail, and your web server falls to an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) or Intentional Insider Threat, it is possible for a hacker to read data after the server decrypts the HTTPs data, but before your server-side code executes to encrypt it for storage inside of your database.  Or, it is possible for the hacker to analyze your application and reverse engineer its encryption method to decrypt the database.  This is where Client-Side Encryption comes in. If you encrypt data in the browser before you send it, and then store that data in the database without ever decrypting it first, it will prevent the webserver from ever having the opportunity to see an unencrypted version of your data no matter how badly compromised the server is.
Based on your description it sounds like your senior developer was going for this, but probably did not do a good job of it.
Client-Side Encryption generally requires a second key server on a different network or persistent local storage capabilities on the client's machine.  Persistent local storage is not something browsers are designed for; so, unless you are using an App, you are probably using a Key-Server.
The way it should work is that the web-server should have the key-server generate a random key for each user which the key server remembers, but the web-server does not. This way, when you go to retrieve your data, instead of relying on the web hosting server to fully decrypt your data, the key server sends the decryption key to the client without ever letting the web server know what that key looks like.  This way, even if the hacker fully reverse engineers your system and tracks every byte of data coming and going from your web-server, he does not have what he needs to read your database.  Inversely, if the key server ever becomes compromised, there is no web application or database on that network to decrypt with it.  So unless the same hacker takes full control of both servers, your data remains secure.
That said, CSE can not take the place of HTTPs either.  In order to function, your application server will need to be able to store at least some of its data in a unencrypted manner. So, things like key IDs, searchable data fields, etc. will typically need to be unencrypted on the web hosting server for the web application to be able know what data to send to the browser.  So, even with certain data being client-side encrypted, you still need HTTPs to secure the stuff for transport that you for practical reasons can not client-side encrypt.
Compartmentalisation: The way it should work is that the web-server should have the key-server generate a random key for each user which the key server remembers, but the web-server does not. This explicitly describes separating key management from data storage, ensuring that no single entity can access both at the same time. "This way, even if the hacker fully reverse engineers your system and tracks every byte of data coming and going from your web-server, he does not have what he needs to read your database." This explains how compartmentalisation limits damage, requiring an attacker to compromise multiple components rather than just one.

Ctrl + V isn't the keys that allow application access to clipboard, because it already have access to the clipboard. It just pastes the data on a field, or transfers it somewhere, because the data is always accessible to it.

The gold standard is to completely avoid this scheme. Not only is the usability terrible, as browsermator already pointed out. The check also cannot withstand offline attacks, no matter how sophisticated the solution may be. You've already explained yourself how the check can be exploited for a very efficient brute-force attack (by iteratively guessing three characters at a time). There might be a way to implement the check with homomorphic or searchable encryption, which would then allow the server to offload it to a hardware security module (HSM) with a non-extractable key and its own rate limiting (so that offline attacks aren't possible). There are also approaches which use Shamir's Secret Sharing.  But I'm not convinced this is how it's done in practice. The phrase is probably just encrypted server-side or even stored as plaintext.

Allowing users to execute custom JavaScript within your website poses significant security challenges, primarily due to the risk of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. To mitigate these risks, consider the following approaches:
1. Isolate Execution with Sandboxed IFrames:
Utilize an  with the sandbox attribute to create a restricted environment for running user-generated scripts. The sandbox attribute can be configured to limit the capabilities of the content within the iframe. For example:
<iframe src="user_script.html" sandbox="allow-scripts"></iframe>

This setup permits script execution within the iframe but prevents actions like form submissions, top-level navigation, and plugin use. It's crucial to note that the allow-scripts directive also disables forms and top-level navigation unless explicitly allowed.
2. Implement a Strict Content Security Policy (CSP):
Define a CSP to control the sources from which content can be loaded and executed. This policy helps prevent the execution of unauthorized scripts. For instance, to restrict script execution to your domain and its subdomains:
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' *.yourdomain.com;

This directive ensures that only scripts from your domain and specified subdomains are executed, mitigating the risk of malicious code injection.

What is the benefit of this indirection?

You have one credential to secure and rotate, even if the application needs many credentials. This makes it easier to follow good practices.
In addition, the vault can be configured to lock down in certain conditions, for instance based on IDS metrics, thus denying access to secrets. Again, centralization makes it easier to secure, as you only have to worry about securing and interfacing one component to the IDS.

In addition to the centralization and lock down benefits mentioned by @vidarlo, secret stores offer some other advantages:

They allow separation of the actual secret from the credentials, plus additional access controls, such that an attacker who gains the credentials can't actually use them. Consider a secret stored in a file, and then that file is present in a backup, and somebody steals the backup tapes or throws them out without destroying their data first and the attacker goes through their trash (pretty common scenarios, sadly). If that secret is something directly usable to the attacker - for example, a secret used to authenticate to your cloud provider for deployments - you're hosed. If that secret is instead an authentication token - a credential - for your vault, then (assuming you didn't screw up horribly and make the vault accessible outside of your secure network) - the attacker can't do anything with that until they compromise your network security or similar.
They allow authorization methods other than authentication. For example, the secret needed to authenticate to the production DB might be released only to the IP range used for the production servers. Ideally you'd also have authentication on top of this, but with restrictions like that your prod DB would hopefully stay safe even if an attacker was able to steal the vault credential and submit requests to the vault itself.
They allow the use of non-exportable secrets. For example, suppose that instead of a DB that wants a static password embedded in a connection string, you're transferring sensitive data from one system to another over a potentially-compromised channel (or storing them for a time over which you fear compromise). If both systems can access the same vault, or if you generate the same secret once and store it in each system's different vault and then destroy all other copies, then one service (e.g. the app server) can encrypt data for the database, and the database can decrypt it, both using a key that doesn't exist anywhere else. Obviously if you are able to intercept the ciphertext and then impersonate (to the vault) the recipient, then you can get it to decrypt the data for you, but you need ongoing access to the vault every time you do this (which may be subject to lock down); you can't just steal the decryption key and then use it directly on whatever data you compromise. Hashicorp specifically talks about this use case.
You can use them to generate, store, and operate on asymmetric private keys. This is technically a special case of the prior bullet point, but it's really important. Ideally, private keys never leave the hardware they're generated on, certainly not in plain text; at most one instance of the private key ever exists. Obviously that key can be used directly to provide security functionality; for example, maybe the credential to access the DB is a JWT signed with a private key known only to the vault; now the DB doesn't even need access to the vault (it can verify the signature using the public key), and an attacker who compromises this setup - even total compromise such that they can execute code as the app server and thus ask the vault to sign whatever they want - can't exfiltrate the private key and will lose the ability to use it as soon as their access is cut off. But such private keys can also be used to encrypt data in a way that provides perfect forward secrecy, by using the private key only to authenticate an ephemeral key exchange (e.g. using ECDHE), such that it is both difficult to steal the key in realtime (because of the security measures around accessing the vault), and useless to steal it (or even gain access to it through e.g. compromising the app server) after the fact; you may have intercepted the ciphertext at some point in the past, but the decryption key for that data simply does not exist anymore.


To be clear, none of these are sure-fire solutions to secret management. Those basically just don't exist. Instead, it's all about raising the bar. If your system is hard enough to attack, attackers will go after an easier target even though you are not actually invulnerable, or at least breach you much less often because each attempt takes a while to reach fruition and costs a lot of resources.
Each of these protections will make some attacks unsuccessful, or at least much costlier. Somebody who gets an XXE that lets them read files through the app server might be able to read all on-disk data including the vault credential, and be able to submit requests to all endpoints the app server can reach including the vault itself, but if they can't put the vault credential into an Authorization: bearer header that the vault expects (XXE generally doesn't let you control headers), they can't actually access the vault in a useful way. Somebody who spends a long time quietly working their way into a target organization to steal the secrets it occasionally transmits to other orgs but gets detected immediately upon tripping the very sensitive IDS around the vault has wasted all that effort if the vault won't actually give them a decryption key, only sign DH params for an ephemeral key exchange. Even if they do exfiltrate a secret, the ability to then immediately and easily change that secret across the entire org (once the attacker is locked out) means having very little opportunity to use the stolen secret before it becomes worthless.

You can use the same key to encrypt multiple values in a database, but there are several caveats.
First, if you use AES-GCM with random IVs, you have to set a strict limit on the number of invocations. Otherwise, you risk IV collisions which are catastrophic for GCM. The IV is effectively limited to 96 bits because GCM needs to fit both the IV and a 32-bit counter into a 128-bit block. You can calculate the collision probability after a certain number of invocations according to the birthday problem. For example, there's 50% collision chance after around 248 invocations. In real-world applications, you'll want that risk to be much lower. The NIST allows a collision probability of at most 2?ÃÂ??ÃÂ??32, which limits you to 232 invocations. After this, you must rotate the key. A more robust approach is to use the deterministic IV construction from section 8.2.1 of NIST Special Publication 800-38D. In this case, the IV is split into a ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?fixed field?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂª?ÃÂ which should be unique per device or context, and an ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?invocation field?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂª?ÃÂ which can be a simple counter. If you make the IV exactly 96 bits long (e.g., 32 bits for the fixed field and 64 bits for the invocation field), you can actually ensure that there are no collisions, allowing you to invoke the encryption function much more often. For example, with a 64-bit invocation field, you can have 264 invocations with unique IVs. Alternatively, avoid AES-GCM in favor of an algorithm like AES-GCM-SIV which is resistant to nonce-reuse.
Another issue is that encrypting all data directly with a single key makes key rotation very difficult, because you have to decrypt and then encrypt all data with the new key. A better option is to have two keys: A data encryption key (DEK) which encrypts the data and a key encryption key (KEK) which encrypts the DEK. When you rotate the KEK, you only have to re-encrypt the DEK, not all data. For rotating the DEK, assign a unique ID to each key and store this ID together with the ciphertext. Then you can introduce a new DEK whenever necessary and use it to encrypt future data.
Also make sure you're using a secure key store. For example, Linux has the Kernel Key Retention Service which allows you to keep keys in kernel memory rather than putting them into files. Other operating systems have similar services. Note that keys stored in the Kernel Key Retention Service aren't persistent by default. If you have a Trusted Platform Module (TPM), or if your CPU provides a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), you can use Trusted Keys. A Trusted Key is encrypted with a persistent TPM/TEE key and can safely be stored in a file, allowing you to automatically load the key after a reboot. Alternatively, you can derive keys from a passphrase which you manually provide when starting the backend service.
Generating secrets: The comment explicitly explains how to manage encryption keys securely, including key rotation, IV collision risks, and how to structure IVs to prevent reuse. It also references NIST Special Publication 800-38D, which provides best practices for key and IV management. This is a clear explanation of secure secret generation.

Most CVE scores are based on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).
Take the NVD, for example. For newly published CVE records, they accept CVSS v3.x and v4.0 (the latest version.)
CVSS uses a number of metrics to assess the overall severity of vulnerabilities. The NVD also have a calculator which you can play around with.

CVE-2024-10957 has a CVSS3.1 metric of

/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

Which means that it is exploited through a network attack vector, is low complexity, requires no privileges etc.

There is an inherint limitation and loss of information when trying to summarize complex multidimensional information like various aspects of the attack into a single value or score.
This limitiation and information loss starts already in the granularity of the different aspects, like there is no continuum between "low" and "high" attack complexity, but only this binary choice. It continues on the weight these different aspects get in the total score, i.e. how these subscores get computed from the aspects and how the total score is then computed from the subscores,
And it does not help that different experts (and also non-experts with strong opinions) have sometimes different opinions about the different aspects of the rating. Low granularity can sometimes harmonize this (but with information loss) but sometimes aggrevate disagreements when the perceived actual value is between two granularity steps.
It also does not help that there are non-technical aspects involved in these opinions, i.e. the finder of a vulnerability will more likely exaggerate the importance, while the one responsible for the vulnerability is more likely to downplay it. And affected users would often like to downplay it too, especially if some regulations require them to mitigate vulnerabilities with a specific score in a specific time.
So it is definitely not perfect and therefore it is also continuously evolving, i.e. we got through multiple versions of CVSS to calculate the score. But is the best we have so far, because it makes it much easier and faster to prioritize vulnerabilities compared to trying to read and understand all the detailed vulnerability reports.
As for how the score is exactly computed and play around with it see CVSS3 calculator which was used to calculate the score for the vulnerability in question. Or check CVSS4 caclulator for a newer version.

You state that "if they aren't it's trivial for them to start [sending emails from a google IP]", while this is true, it is NOT trivial for them to start sending emails from a google IP with your domain in the from field. Essentially you are building a chain, DMARC ensures the from address matches the envelope address (or the message is signed, which isn't relevant to this discussion), SPF ensures that the envelope address was used by an approved server, and Google's internal security systems ensure that servers only send messages where the address matches an approved domain for the sending user.

Attack scenarios
You should take into account that encryption itself provides confidentiality on the contents, but there are a number of attacks that a malicious admin on that remote machine could perform.
Remove your data.
This may happen with any solution, and is as simple as deleting the files you uploaded. If you store there your only copy of the Coca-Cola formula and an admin deletes it (or your whole account/vps), you lose it, even if the attacker cannot read it.
Corrupt your data
Any of the above solutions will detect a file not uploaded by you. In the PGP case by a failing signature, the encryption filesystems will report an error reading the file.
File exchanging
Someone with access to the vps could rename Bonus_to_be_paid_to_the_CEO.txt.gpg to Bonus_to_be_paid_to_Pedro.txt.gpg (and Pedro's to the CEO), without knowing the actual amount on those text files.
The PGP solution is trivially vulnerable to this, since it does no protection of filenames. encfs and gocryptfs encrypt filenames, but files can still be exchanged blindly. That's also the case with securefs in lite mode, but not in full. CryFS is not susceptible to that.
Back-in-time
An attacker will always be able to revert the status of the store, sometimes selectively per-file (depending on the encryption filesystem and its config) but in any case by restoring everything to a previous version.

note this can happen even if filenames are encrypted, since the attacker would presumably know the time at which the initial contract was uploaded.

The original lookup tables by Hellman (1980) and the refined rainbow table structure by Oechslin (2003) both use elements from the search space as starting and end points. So in the case of password hashes, the tables only consist of passwords.
In the lookup tables suggested by Hellman (which are not Rainbow tables), a chain has the following format when applied to password hashes:
p_0 -(H)-> h_0 -(R)-> p_1 -(H)-> h_1 -(R)-> p_2 -...-> p_t

This means the chain starts with an initial password p_0 which is then hashed with some function H to produce h_0. The hash h_0 is reduced to a password p_1 using a reduction function R. Then p_1 is again hashed etc. until the chain ends at a password p_t.
For each chain, only the first and last passwords p_0 and p_t are stored in a table.
To do a lookup for a given hash h, you first reduce the hash to obtain a password R(h). If this already matches the endpoint pt of a chain, then the hash likely is the last one in the chain, and the password p you're looking for likely is right before that hash:
p0 -(H)-> h0 -(R)-> p1 -...-> p -(H)-> h -(R)-> pt 

So you reconstruct the entire chain from the starting point p0.
If R(h) matches none of the endpoints, then h could still be the second-to-last hash in the chain. So you hash and reduce R(h) to again check the endpoints etc.
Rainbow tables are a different data structure which uses multiple reduction functions, but the basic principle of the lookup is the same.
Instead of passwords, you could use hashes as the endpoints, but this would make the tables bigger. A password is typically much shorter than a cryptographic hash. For example, SHA-512 takes up 64 bytes, whereas passwords are roughly 10 characters long on average (how many bytes this requires depends on the character encoding, of course).
Using hashes as endpoints would also make the lookups slightly awkward. In the above scheme, you start with R(h) and then iteratively apply the composed function f(x) = R(H(x)) until you get a matching endpoint. So it's always a hash step followed by a reduction step. If you stored hashes, then you would need to introduce an extra case where the last iteration only applies H and not R.
On a side note: Rainbow tables (or classical lookup tables) may be historically relevant, but I highly doubt they're still used a lot today. Compared to 1980 or 2003, it's much easier to get massive computing power for a direct brute-force attack through GPUs or specialized hardware like ASICs and FPGAs. And of course lookup tables only work if the hashes aren't salted ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?? which should also become more and more rare.
