As you say yourself, you have no idea which countries are trusted or not.
Most people rely on major OS or browser developers to maintain trusted CA lists based on technical and security assessments, rather than (often prejudiced) geopolitical concerns.
For example, Mozilla publishes its trusted CA list in their Common CA Database, which you can view here.

The current rules are set by CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements.
The rules details how issuer should verify ownership and so forth, and those criteria is what major CA consumers (Microsoft, Google, Mozilla etc) go by - the criteria is agreed upon by the browser vendors (consumers) and certificate providers (CA's), and interested parties.
The question boils down to how much you trust various issuers to not work with the government. That's a tough call to make, and it will probably vary from person to person.

It all depends on the websites visited by your userbase, but that is probably more diverse than you expect.
If this is a server only visiting a single website, specially one under your control as well, then sure. It's fine to restrict that to only a handful of CAs.
If you are running on a tightly restricted company/government where only a few websites are approved, that may be fine.
If you have many users visiting many websites, you will probably hit unexpected usage of CAs. Remember, in theory all of them would be equally good, and you are breaking that expectation.
Perhaps a Chinese CA would be more used by Chinese websites, and your users don't visit Chinese websites. But you could stumble on a web from US, Africa or Europe using a Chinese CA. Maybe simply because they got a cheap offer from that page.
Moreover, this not only involves the websites, but all their dependencies. So, if website example.com loads a script from website example.org, and that one uses a CA not trusted, the result will simply be that example.com does not work.
I have seen a good number of websites that are misconfigured by not serving the intermediate CA certificate. Including by big enough companies that should know better. A missing intermediate CA is a nasty error because:

It depends on the program and OS you are using to access the site.
If you have ever visited before another page using that intermediate CA, the browser has cached it, and won't complain about the misconfiguration.
Some browsers will autodownload the missing Certificate.
Some browsers come with all Intermediates shipped.

The result is that for the people handling that website (and most users) it works. But if it is the first website you access from a clean install it will not. Or if the intermediate CA certificate download is blocked by the firewall.
And so it is hard to convince that they have an issue.
In your case, you are purposefully breaking an unknown number of websites, for everyone but your own company. That's unlikely to go well.
What many companies do is to have some proxying of web traffic. That is mostly targeted for sites serving phishing, malware or even webs in a category not approved by company policy. Sometimes that includes breaking into the https, and others it isn't (or only conditionally). That system could -potentially- include a check like the one you propose.
(The verification done by such proxy if MITM the connection is probably weaker than those modern browsers perform, though, if not much more broken)
However, what you would probably be more interested in would be the statistics of the CAs that are actually being used (which is probably not included).

Focusing now in the worthiness of the different CAs, you should note that their product is based precisely on trust. Trust that they are verifying the owners properly and they don't misbehave. Many of the changes in the last years have also been motivated to be more sure they are doing thing right or helping them to keep them honest.
A big example of this is the Certificate Transparency ecosystem, as are when browsers require that the presented certificate includes a precertificate in order in order to ensure it was logged before trusting it.
Finding a misissued certificate is rare. Although it does happen. And it causes enough questioning to the CA.
A certificate misissued on purpose, by a CA compelled by their government would cause them being quickly expelled (untrusted) from the root programs. Which, in turn, would likely mean the demise of the company selling the certificates.
So, the CA company has a strong incentive not to misissue a certificate. And the country doing that probably knows as well that it is a bullet they probably can only use once.
This doesn't mean there won't ever be malicious certificates, but it (tries to) set a relatively high bar for the PKI to work properly. While you can untrust CA you don't feel safe trusting, I wouldn't recommend doing that blindly, without first checking their actual usage by the target population.
Minimum trust and maximum trustworthines: "A certificate misissued on purpose, by a CA compelled by their government would cause them being quickly expelled (untrusted) from the root programs. Which, in turn, would likely mean the demise of the company selling the certificates." The comment explicitly explains how Certificate Authorities (CAs) are incentivized to maintain trust by following security policies, and how Certificate Transparency helps ensure their trustworthiness.

Comment:
Yes, you could replace PKCE with a signature-based proof-of-possession scheme, but this would only lead to more complexity and a bigger risk of errors in the protocol design.
Hash calculations are very simple compared to calculating a signature. In fact, before you can sign a message, you first have to hash it. So using signatures to avoid hashing makes no sense.
Additionally, just signing a client-chosen random value doesn't bind the key to the particular authorization token. If an attacker ever manages to obtain any signature from the victim, they could send it along an arbitrary authorization code and pretend this is a fresh proof-of-possession referring to this code. This may even work multiple times if the authorization server doesn't keep track of the random values that have already been sent. For proper proof of possession, the client would either have to sign the authorization token itself or a server-chosen random value.
PKCE is a much simpler scheme which is easier to get right. And as already pointed out, it doesn't introduce any additional cryptographic operations.

GnuPG stores all public keys and metadata (regardless of whether or not the private part is known) in a key database. This can either be an SQLite database or a GPG-specific file (called pubring.kbx or pubring.gpg; the former uses the new keybox format, the latter is a legacy file). When you call gpg --list-secret-keys, then the key information is read from this database, and only then is the GPG agent queried to check whether the private part exists (in the folder private-keys-v1.d).
If gpg --list-keys doesn't show the keys at all, then there's a problem with the key database ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?? maybe it wasn't backed up properly, or maybe you're using two different GPG versions. If gpg --list-keys shows the keys but gpg --list-secret-keys doesn't, then it's an issue with private-keys-v1.d.
If the key database is broken, you can try to restore the public keys and metadata from a key server (or any person you've sent this data to). You can also get the public part from the private-keys-v1.d files, and you might be able to gather enough information to reconstruct the metadata ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?? though this isn't worth the effort if you can just generate new keys.
But as dave_thompson_085 already said, the proper solution for future backups is to export the keys and not rely on any internal GPG databases. The formats used internally can change at any time, and there's no guarantee you can just copy the files to a new GPG instance.

If you allow the null origin, this is effectively even more lax than the wildcard *. Any document can create a null origin, e.g., by loading a data: URL. Additionally, null origins can make credentialed requests, which isn't possible if the wildcard is used. The W3C specifically recommends against allowing the null origin, so you should not use this as a workaround.
The proper solution is to remove the sandbox directive, set the default-src to 'none' and then whitelist the font URL through font-src. You can further restrict the page if appropriate, e.g., by disabling form submissions with form-action 'none'.

BitLocker uses multiple keys. The data on the disk is encrypted with a Full Volume Encryption Key (FVEK). Bitlocker then encrypts the FVEK with a Volume Master Key (VMK) and the VMK with a key protector ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?? like a TPM. The VMK is only decrypted if you've passed the checks of the key protector. But after you've done that, yes, the VMK resides in RAM as plaintext and can be dumped given sufficient permissions.
So the TPM doesn't do the actual disk encryption and therefore cannot hide the VMK from the (unlocked) system. It was never designed for this purpose and is far too slow to process large amounts of data. Instead, the TPM can be used in conjunction with Secure Boot to check the integrity of the operating system and only release the VMK if this check has passed. This is exactly what BitLocker does. In other words, the point of a TPM is to protect the VMK as long as the system is locked, not afterwards.

As @Ja1024 mentions, the TPM is only used as a "protector" to unlock the VMK, which in turn is used to decrypt the VMEK, which lives in (kernel) memory. So regarding question 1, Yes, the key to decrypt the disk is loaded into RAM, generally speaking. (One possible exception is for drives with on-board encryption hardware; I don't know how those work exactly but plausibly the key for them is passed directly from the CPU registers to the appropriate I/O address for the drive, and never actually stored in physical RAM.)
For your second question, there are a number of practical benefits to the use of a TPM with Bitlocker:

The TPM protects against modification of the pre-boot code (e.g. tampering with the bootloader, which of course lives in plain text). Even knowing what the pre-boot code should be, it would be very difficult to make the TPM cough up the Bitlocker protector key if the actual boot code is modified. This greatly raises the bar for "evil maid" attacks or similar, which could otherwise do things like install a keylogger in the bootloader. Combined with Secure Boot, this ensures the integrity of the entire boot process, before and after unlocking the encrypted volume.
Unlike boot-time "PINs"[1], there is no practical way to attack the TPM protector offline. The TPM is strongly tamper-resistant and only a very sophisticated attacker would have a realistic chance of extracting the key while the device is "cold", even knowing the expected sequence of extensions into the PCRs.
The TPM doesn't depend on human-memorable secrets. People are terrible at choosing passwords, much less numeric PINs, and tend to reuse them. An attacker who knows the likely PINs/passwords of their victim through some means (e.g. breached password lists, https://xkcd.com/792/, shoulder surfing, etc.) can potentially guess the Bitlocker PIN easily, even if the attacker doesn't actually know it. Obviously the TPM only helps here if either only the drive (not the whole computer) is available to the attacker, or the attacker doesn't know the OS password and can't pull off a hardware (e.g. cold boot) attack, but that does cover a number of cases (e.g. disposal of old drives, theft of backup mirrors, etc.)
TPM-only mode (which is actually the default) can provide moderate protection to the machine's data without requiring a boot-time password at all. While requiring a second factor (a memorized secret "PIN" or a key stored on a removable drive) obviously increases security, Windows does its best to remain secure with TPM-only mode (e.g. restricting DMA, especially before user login), assuming that the OS user login password isn't known to the attacker (and the use of Bitlocker, even only with the TPM, prevents the kind of disk-modification attacks usually used to bypass the OS login security). This is much more convenient than requiring a boot PIN, especially if the device may be used by multiple users or may run without a keyboard connected.


[1] By default, Bitlocker only supports numeric PINs for boot-time memorized secrets. While the reasoning for this choice makes some sense - the pre-boot code doesn't know what keyboard layout the OS uses, but the digits and especially the F-keys are the same keyboard codes for all languages and layouts - it's lazy and IMO badly designed. A simple fix would be to have an option - one that doesn't require using the freaking Group Policy Editor or manually changing registry values - to say "let me use non-numeric values anyhow", with an explanation of the risks. A smarter option would be to automatically convert the keyboard input to what the bootloader keyboard driver would use when recording the Bitlocker password, with a warning to the user that if they ever connect a different keyboard they will need to hit the same keys, rather than enter the same text. Alternatively they could stuff support for different keyboard layouts into the bootloader, and let the user specify when they're using a different one.

A TPM protector enables unattended decryption/startup of the host using a single BitLocker protector. If that is what you want.
This is vulnerable to interception on the low pin count bus so it should not be used on hosts that aren't physically secure (mobile).
TPM is also used for recording and measurement of various aspects of the host during startup to ensure it hasn't changed or been compromised (attestation).

We can only speculate about the reasoning behind this design decision ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?? there may also be no particular reason at all. The website owners might simply assume that the purpose is obvious from the context and doesn't have be explicitly stated.
From a security perspective, there's no good reason to omit the purpose. In fact, this would be classical security through obscurity. An attacker who has already managed to obtain a code will have no trouble finding out what the code is used for. They likely know the receiver's e-mail address or phone number. Based on this information, they can find out the account and simply try different actions with the code.
In practice, it's also not very likely that an attacker just stumbles upon a code by accident. Instead, attackers who are in a man-in-the-middle position will purposely trigger e-mail/SMS messages to obtain the code. Then they already know what they're for.

One thing to consider is that people can make typos, including on the mobile number that they enter when signing up to new services. If they enter their number incorrectly and some person gets a message that says "Your verification code is 123456", they can potentially work out which service it came from based on the sender, but not much else.
But if instead they get a text saying "Here is the code to register your account with this email address" then you're exposing the legitimate user's email address to them, and with a username + phone number they're more likely to be able to go through account recovery processes (or social engineering attacks against the service), which could allow them to gain access to the account.
So by including that extra information in the SMS message, you're creating an opportunity for it to be accidentally exposed. And you're also increasing the amount of personal data that's getting send via a third party and SMS (although mobile numbers would often be considered personal data anyway).

Stating the action can improve security in some scenarios.
Imagine paying a bill, with a trojan on your computer. If the SMS message simply says Your verification code is 123456, you have no way of detecting that the trojan submits a different account number than what the browser shows you.
However, if the SMS message includes account number and amount, it is possible to detect such attacks.
The same goes for when sender is a random number, and not text or commonly known. A 3rd party site could possibly claim that the code is for that site, while it's in reality for e.g. facebook or whatever. Including the service name and action would allow detection of such attacks.

Frame Challenge: What happens when someone ignores a verification code?
If, as an application, you send a valid verification code, but someone just...doesn't use it in the expected timeframe, then it just...expires.
You could also set it up so that, when a second request is made, the first verification code, even though not expired yet, is now inoperable. Or maybe they both work?
But in general, the intent is that you go from getting a verification code sent to immediately using said verification code.
If you do not understand where the verification code is coming from, it is better practice to just delete/ignore it, letting it expire.
If someone else is tripping your MFA notification/text messages, and it is not you, it would be better for you to not provide it anywhere. Classical practice is to not send your password to someone claiming to be a member of the organization's support team, nor is it something you should be sharing with others asking you to pass on their verification code; if they mis-typed the phone number to send it to, for example, it is better for them to have to re-input their phone number to get their SMS code sent to their number.
To that end, stating the purpose can give users a false sense of confidence that they should use the code, when regardless of where they get the code from, it should not work for where they are planning to use it unless it is where they should be using it, and an incorrect code indicates that it does not give access to the tool they thought it would.

This answer is written with the assumption that you're asking how an app or website can authenticate a user's fingerprint, when the user logs in using biometrics. If you mean some other scenario, such as a police detective comparing fingerprints found at a crime scene, sorry for the confusion.

One thing that is very important to note here, and that you might be missing, is that no consumer fingerprint reader (that I'm aware of) sends the fingerprint data anywhere. It only compares it against an internal store of specific characteristics, and - if it matches - then releases a stored credential (could be a a random token, a cryptographic key, etc.) to the [connected/rest of the] device. Both the actual fingerprint scan, and the characteristics used to recognize a particular fingerprint, are only ever stored in the scanner module itself.
When you sign into an app with a fingerprint, the app never sees the fingerprint data, or anything directly associated with it. Instead, the app asks the OS "hey, I want to authenticate the user, please turn on the biometric scanner". The OS does so, signaling the scanner with an authentication challenge. The user touches the scanner, which captures the print and looks it up against its stored characteristics of enrolled prints. If there's a match, the scanner responds to the OS's challenge with a "yep, it's user X, here's their associated credential". The OS verifies the response, validates the credential, and then signals the app "yep, it's that user, you can proceed".
Similar flows happen when signing into the device itself (there's no "app" other than the OS's own login screen, and the OS creates an OS user session itself upon confirming the identity), or when logging into a website or similar via FIDO2/webauthn (there's an extra step there where the site or other FIDO2 "relying party" presents a challenge that the OS cryptographically signs after validating the user's identity, and this signed response is what gets sent to the relying party). In no case does the actual fingerprint data go anywhere, though.
So, to answer your question for the specific context of fingerprint authentication in software, Bob doesn't need to trust that X is a physical representation of Alice's fingerprint, because Alice's fingerprint reader never sends fingerprint data to Bob (or anywhere else). Instead, Bob must trust that Alice's device is truthfully reporting when Alice uses the fingerprint reader. For local (same-device) versions of the situation, where "Bob" is an app on Alice's device, this can just be a "yep, that's Alice" message coming from the OS; you don't have to worry about spoofing or interception, because any bad actor who could do that could completely take over the device including "Bob". For the remote case (passkeys and other FIDO2 authentication), "Bob" (the remote server) holds a public key generated by Alice['s device], and uses it to verify that the client holds Alice's corresponding private key; this works great for authentication, but doesn't actually prove that Alice used her fingerprint to unlock that private key (FIDO2 authenticators can - and some do - lie about how the user was authenticated).
(This is also why Charlie can't use their fingerprint on Alice's device to log into Charlie's account on an app or website. Alice's fingerprint reader doesn't recognize Charlie's fingerprint or have a credential to release for Charlie, and Alice's device doesn't have Charlie's FIDO2 private key. If the reader was just returning the fingerprint data, and it was sent to the app or server directly, then a user would only need to ever enroll their print once, on any device, and then they could use it to log into that app/site on all devices forevermore, no matter who owns them.)
Compartmentalisation: "No consumer fingerprint reader (that I?m aware of) sends the fingerprint data anywhere. It only compares it against an internal store of specific characteristics, and - if it matches - then releases a stored credential (could be a random token, a cryptographic key, etc.) to the [connected/rest of the] device." Defines an explicit security mechanism: The fingerprint scanner itself isolates the biometric data and does not expose it externally.

OSes in common use all have such "super admin" capabilities. Clearly, the regular user does not have such privileges and even the administrative user(s) should minimize their use of escalated privilege. This principle is called "least privilege" and some of the other answers cover it in detail. Minimizing privilege use is obviously a "best practice" for the security conscious administrator.

This capability is removed in high security specialized operating systems with a practice called "two person control." Typically, admin accounts have all the normal privileges one associates with them now, but a separate security admin account also exists. Regular admin accounts make security-sensitive privilege changes BUT those changes do not go into effect until approved by a security admin account. A security admin account cannot make privilege or ownership changes, but only approve or disapprove changes made by a regular admin. By restricting those roles to different people, you prevent a single person from having the "super admin" capability.

Ping uses a special kind of IP (Internet Protocol) packet known as ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), as opposed to the much-more-common UDP (User Datagram Protocol, used for broadcast messages or anything where minimal overhead is needed) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol, used everywhere reliable delivery is needed including most web traffic).
The Linux kernel (and other operating systems too) does not by default allow arbitrary processes to generate or receive ICMP traffic; instead, it is generated by low-level network drivers and hardware (and responded to at the same layer), well below the visibility of user applications. Thus, either ping needs special permissions to generate arbitrary IP packets (this is why, on many Linux systems, the ping binary is marked SetUID root... but of course that doesn't work on rootless environments) or the kernel must be re-configured to allow unprivileged processes to generate and receive ICPM traffic.
On modern Linux, there are a number of "capabilities" that control kernel-enforced privileges. Try man 7 capabilities (or see https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html) to read about them and view the list. Some network-relevant ones are:

CAP_NET_ADMIN, which allows controlling a bunch of network configuration stuff and is usually used by firewalls, VPNs, and tools like NetworkManager.
CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, which bypasses the usual restriction on listening at TCP or UDP ports below 1024 and is used by server processes that want to listen on well-known ports without needing arbitrary root privileges, such as web and DNS servers.
CAP_NET_RAW, which allows crafting and listening to network packets using arbitrary protocols, including ICMP; one of the main users is ping.

A simple way to give a process such capabilities is to have it run as root, since by default the root user has access to all capabilities (though this can be restricted, and is in various containers or sandboxes). However, root has for more privileges (both in terms of capabilities, and in terms of file system / object access) than most processes need, so it's a violation of the principle of least privilege to run things as root just because they need e.g. raw packet access. Thus, capabilities create a way to grant much more fine-grained and limited privileges, so fewer processes need to run as root. Processes can also drop capabilities after they no longer need them (e.g. a web server could bind to local TCP ports 80 and 443, and then drop the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability before it starts handling requests so that even if the server is compromised, it doesn't even have that privilege anymore.

As for why unprivileged apps aren't allowed to use ICMP, the short answer is that normal apps have no legitimate use for ICMP traffic (which is mostly for error handling, some but not all of which is the sort that causes the OS to report various error codes) so, by principle of least privilege, they can't use it. This isn't actually a restriction about ICMP at all; there are several protocols available on top of IP (and more protocol numbers that could be standardized to mean various new transports). The expectation is that if a program is using IP, it's probably able to do anything it needs via TCP or UDP, so giving it access to anything else is unnecessary risk. The fact that Ping (and Traceroute) are thus impaired is an unfortunate historical fact.
An incomplete list of specific attacks that can occur if programs are able to use ICMP or other non-TCP, non-UDP protocols:

ICMP is used for error reporting, and a malicious program could report nonexistent errors along particular network paths. This might cause other programs to be unable to reach their destination hosts, or even the entire machine to incorrectly think the network is down.
ICMP can be used for various attacks on servers, such as ping floods, misdirection attacks (where the attacker sends a ping which lies about its origin, and the router or destination server sends the response to another IP, increasing the target's network congestion and load), and overly-large packets that recipients fail to handle, such as the classic "ping of death". Obviously anybody on the Internet could be sending those at any time, so Internet-facing services need to be prepared for them, but inside a controlled environment (e.g. a corporate LAN), you might expect that such attacks won't occur because you haven't given any untrusted users root privileges and don't allow untrusted devices on the network.
ARP (Address Routing Protocol) is used to associate MAC (physical) addresses to IP addresses on a LAN. A malicious process able to spoof ARP traffic can convince other machines on the same LAN that it - rather than the router - is the network gateway (by e.g. telling them that 192.168.0.1 maps to their own MAC address) and convince the router that the other machines' IP addresses are all actually located on its own IP address. The attacker thus gains a "man in the middle" position for all Internet traffic that the target machines send or receive, enabling many attacks. While this is hard to prevent in environments where arbitrary machines can connect to the network (e.g. a coffee shop), it's another case where a secure network such as a corporate LAN might assume no malicious code has the privileges required.
ARP spoofing can of course also be used to just block other machines off of the network, or prevent them from communicating with specific network peers.

The key concept is that if an attacker with admin rights on your systems can destroy all your backups (which ransomware groups are known to do), then they don't really protect you against a ransomware attack. So you need a backup that cannot be destroyed, even with full administrative rights.
If you go back a few years, people used to talk about the concept of offline backups, which were stored somewhere that was physically disconnected from your live systems (often on portable hard drives or tapes, and ideally also stored in a separate physical location). And those protect against the ransomware issue, because even if all my systems are compromised and an attacker can destroy everything online, they can't touch the tapes in a fireproof safe.
But with more and more stuff moving to the cloud, having offline backups is difficult (or expensive) for many people, so providers have implemented immutable backups to try and achieve the same thing - a backup that you can restore from, but that is impossible for an attacker who's compromised your account to destroy.
The main concern that a lot of people have around this approach is that you're really just having to trust the third party when they say it's "immutable" and can't be deleted - so you don't have the same level of confidence that you would have in knowing that your backups are physically disconnected and stored in a locked box somewhere. And of course, the immutable backups don't necessarily protect against other things (like your backup provider going out of business, or suffering hardware failures/site outages/etc).
So the question you should really be asking is: if we get compromised, how can I stop the ransomware group destroying all my backups as well?
Immutable backups on a third party system are one possible answer to that, but they're not the only one.

In terms of security architecture, a longer path length has no advantage for the security of the device itself, but it has an advantage for the security of the network as a whole, because it allows delegation and compartmentalization. The short version of the answer is "you should be asking this on crypto.stackexchange.com", because it's fundamentally a question about how cryptography works, not about security APIs. To put it differently, the API works that way because that's what those primitives can be used for.
To answer your specific points:

RSA with Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding is intended for encryption use, not for other uses. Padding is an essential part of securely encrypting with RSA; naive encryption with a bare RSA key has serious pitfalls. Similarly, RSA with Probabilistic Signature Scheme is a way to securely handle signing with RSA. You can use the same underlying keypair for both (or for PKCS v1.5 if you really must, but you shouldn't, it's obsolete), but the way they are used is different. From a programmer's perspective, RSA-OAEP public keys are a subclass of Asymmetric Encryption Public Keys, and implement the relevant API; RSA-PSS public keys are subclasses of Digital Signature Public Key (as are Ed25519 public keys) and have a different API from encryption public keys.
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm is an algorithm for signing (and verifying signatures), not for encryption. RSA can use the same keys and ~same algorithm for both operations, but that's not universal (and it requires huge key sizes and computationally expensive math to do so securely). Ed25519 is a specific case of the EdDSA (guess what the "DSA" part stands for there) family, also designed specifically for signing/verifying. There do exist elliptic curve algorithms for asymmetric encryption and decryption - see ECIES, the Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme - but that's a different algorithm.
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman is - like all Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithms - intended neither to encrypt nor to sign date, but instead to allow two parties to mutually agree on an unpredictable secret without revealing the secret to eavesdroppers. Thus, it's usable for deriving a (symmetric) key or other random bitstring - because that's fundamentally what it does, calling it a "key exchange" is arguably a misnomer, the key doesn't exist until the algorithm completes - but not for anything else (though Integrated Encryption Scheme is built on the same computational "problem" that secures DH key exchanges). Note that you can use asymmetric encryption algorithms for securely transmitting a pre-generated key (or other secret) to the other party - this is how RSA is used for key exchanges - but it's less secure, because the sender must encrypt the secret to a public key that has a corresponding private key held by the recipient, and that private key is generally persistent such that it could be compromised later and used to decrypt the secret. DH-based key exchanges usually use "ephemeral" parameters (or "keys") that generated, used once, and then discarded; there is no persisted value that could retroactively be used to compromise the exchanged key.
Generating secrets: The comment explicitly describes how cryptographic keys are generated and used, including Diffie-Hellman key exchanges to derive unpredictable secrets and RSA for key transmission. It explains why ephemeral keys improve security by ensuring no persistent private key can be compromised later. This aligns with the principle of secure secret generation.

It is not unusual that malware comes in encrypted form and then has a stub so it can self-decrypt. But this is not what you seem to ask about. You instead ask if malware can do harm if it is encrypted out of control of the malware.
In general, malware always needs some execution environment to do harm. It is not by itself dangerous if it just stored in a database, at an USB stick, as a string inside a program, in an environment variable, as a comment inside the image meta data, as a part of a web request ... - as long as nothing takes it from there and executes it.
Such execution might be intentionally by executing the file, but it might be unintentionally due to security issues of loading DLL from untrusted places, by making wrong assumptions about the input which lead to code injections like buffer overflow, SQL injection, OS command injection, XSS, ...
This is true no matter if the malware is in plain or encrypted or encoded or somehow else changed in a reversible way. Encryption or encoding just add a barrier for accidental execution - as long as the decryption/decoding part is not executed too.
So could one construct an environment where encrypted malware poses a risk? Sure, if the environment has access to the decryption keys and can be somehow tricked (bugs, social attacks, ...) to use these keys to decrypt the malware and then execute it. But without access to the decryption keys it cannot decrypt the malware and execute it.
But the encrypted bytes of the malware themselves pose no risk, when there is no execution environment which can decrypt and execute it.

The TLS specifications clearly define which messages must be sent and received in which order for the handshake to succeed. If two peers screw this up by trying to interleave two handshakes, then the handshake(s) will fail.
For example, RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) states:

Protocol messages MUST be sent in the order defined in Section 4.4.1
and shown in the diagrams in Section 2.  A peer which receives a
handshake message in an unexpected order MUST abort the handshake
with an "unexpected_message" alert.

But this kind of confusion should not happen, because both parties must already have established a TCP connection before they can start the TLS handshake (leaving aside TLS variants like the UDP-based DTLS). For that, one party (the server) must listen for incoming connections on a particular socket, and the other (the client) must initiate the connection. In the worst case, both peers would unexpectedly end up with two separate TCP and TLS connections where the client/server roles are reversed, but this needs to be fixed in the P2P protocol and isn?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?ÃÂt a problem of TLS.

The Reddit thread that you link to seems to answer the question: there is a specific list of cryptographic algorithms that have been validated and approved by NIST, and ChaCha20 is not on that list.
https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-algorithm-validation-program
Validating cryptographic algorithms takes time (and money), and involves a lot of bureaucratic overheads. So unless there is a strong business case for NIST to invest resources in doing so for a specific algorithm, it will never end up on their approval list, regardless of it's actual security.
And that does not mean that there is necessarily anything wrong with the algorithm, or that it is insecure. And it should also be noted that something being approved by NIST also does not necessarily mean that it is secure (see the infamous case of DUAL_EC_DRBG).
It just means that one specific organisation in the USA has not validated and approved its usage (potentially for their own benefit rather than yours) - so if you are required to only use NIST approved algorithms then it would not be compliant. And if you aren't required to only use NIST approved algorithms, then you shouldn't worry about it.

ChaCha20 is a stream cipher, and there currently isn't any NIST-approved stream cipher at all. The only option is the block cipher AES (Triple DES and Skipjack are only approved for legacy decryption). Of course AES can be (and almost always is) used in a mode of operation like GCM which makes it behave like a stream cipher, but it's still a block cipher.
The topic of standardizing a stream cipher especially for resource-constrainted environments has been discussed within the NIST since at least 2011. In the Lightweight Crypto Standardization Process, there was at least one stream cipher (Grain-128AEAD) which made it to the final round, but ultimately, it lost to a block cipher.
So the NIST doesn't reject stream ciphers, nor have they (as far as I'm aware) ever recommended against ChaCha20 in particular. It's just that the algorithm hasn't gone through any NIST standardization process. I'm not even sure if Bernstein ever tried, so the chances of a FIPS approval anytime soon seem slim ?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?? regardless of whether or not ChaCha20 is a good cipher.

No. Modifying the client-side version of the site has no meaningful security impact; a secure site doesn't trust the client, and thus any site where a modification of the client-side code could bypass a security control is already, inherently, insecure. An attacker could mock up their own .HTML file that interacts with the insecure server, or simply use tools like curl or even telnet to communicate with it directly, and do anything that any client-side code could do.
Phishing is similarly not a risk, unless you've made some truly terrible security decisions. There's no point in modifying a site to phish yourself, of course, any more than there's any point in using the developer console to "XSS" yourself. Attacks are things you do to others. However, since the local version of the site is user-specific, modifying it won't affect any other users, even on the same computer. If you can modify what another user sees, you already have vast privileges than compromise them; presenting a phishing page might be worthwhile if you don't yet have their credentials, but you could also just inject a keylogger or various other attacks. The only reason modification of a local copy of a web page would be a phishing risk is if multiple people share a common login session of the same user account on a given computer, which is a drastically insecure thing to do and can't be meaningfully made secure.
Similarly, while browser extensions can indeed both store data and modify pages, they can also execute arbitrary script and act somewhat outside of the usual browser security controls; a malicious one isn't quite as bad as running a malicious executable directly, but can still do tremendous harm. If your victim has installed a malicious extension, you don't need to mess around with modifying local copies of web pages; you can directly inject spyware into their browsing activity, modify the content they see or download, and otherwise take essentially full control of their experience in anything related to the Web.

Trying to imagine why an IT admin would block the use of the browser dev tools (or at least, block modifications through them, which also requires blocking the console). There's no good reason, but companies do stupid stuff for bad reasons all the time. One possibility is if they send secrets (that the user isn't supposed to know) in the network content (e.g. in the HTML, or in a cookie, or whatever) and they want to prevent you from seeing them. This is stupid on several different levels and easy enough to bypass, but maybe they think the speed bump of effort is enough to dissuade people. Alternatively, maybe you are sharing a common login session, and IT thinks they've restricted the machine enough to prevent other cross-user compromise (they haven't). The possibility is some kind of extreme principle of least privilege, if they went through the group policy editor and simply blocked every policy of the form "allow the user to..." except for ones needed for very specific tasks, which is... extremely paranoid but I can't deny that I respect the idea.

The point of OAuth is that a resource server delegates the task of client authentication and authorization to a dedicated server instead of doing this itself. If you don't want delegation, that's fine. You don't need OAuth with its access tokens then. Use classical API tokens, TLS client certificates or other methods to directly authenticate the client towards the resource server.
However, if you do want to delegate authorization, then a client which has been authorized by the dedicated authorization server needs a way to convey this information to the resource server. This is what access tokens are for. An access token can, for example, be a JSON Web Token which contains a set of claims signed by the authorization server (e.g., the exact permissions which the server has granted). The resource server only has to check the signature and can then trust the claims.

There are indirect constraints
The OpenID Connect 1.0 section 2 limits the specification to ASCII characters:

sub REQUIRED. Subject Identifier. A locally unique and never reassigned identifier within the Issuer for the End-User, which is intended to be consumed by the Client, e.g., 24400320 or AItOawmwtWwcT0k51BayewNvutrJUqsvl6qs7A4. It MUST NOT exceed 255 ASCII characters in length. The sub value is a case sensitive string.

However, there are further indirect restrictions as they are JSON Web Tokens (JWT) defined in RFC 7519, relying on JSON strings and their formatting. Using control characters (ASCII 0?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ??31) would violate the rules for JSON strings defined in RFC 8259, 7, matching exactly the RFC 4627, 2.5 that was present when RFC 7519 was written, but not referenced in it.

The representation of strings is similar to conventions used in the C
family of programming languages.  A string begins and ends with
quotation marks.  All Unicode characters may be placed within the
quotation marks, except for the characters that MUST be escaped:
quotation mark, reverse solidus, and the control characters (U+0000
through U+001F).

Instead, RFC 8259, 4.1.2 defines the sub as StringOrURI and section 2 adds a constraint:

StringOrURI. A JSON string value, with the additional requirement that while arbitrary string values MAY be used, any value containing a : character MUST be a URI [RFC3986].

As control characters are non-printable and not part of the reserved or unreserved characters defined in RFC 3986 2.2 & 2.3, they must be percent-escaped (2.1).
Sanitize control characters
Although OpenID Connect does not specifically ban control characters, their inclusion in the sub claim could lead to security risks, including injection attacks, XSS, data corruption, and problems with interoperability. To ensure robust security and minimize vulnerabilities, it is advisable to prevent control characters from entering the sub claim and to properly sanitize any user inputs.
From a security perspective, sanitizing the sub claim (i.e., removing or replacing control characters) is the most robust approach because it ensures control characters do not enter the system in the first place. Simply escaping them may introduce situations where they are later unescaped and treated as special characters, potentially leading to unintended behavior.

The (discrete) entropy is in IT sometimes easy to misunderstand. In general the entropy metric describes the amount of possible states of a system. In IT world that means, that the entropy of a piece of data is the minimal number of bytes, which is required to represent this data.
That means, that the entropy of a password is the theoretical lower bound of effort for a brute- force attack (now ignoring dictionary lookups). If your password has for example an entropy of n bits, the expected lowest bound of combinations an attacker has to iterate by brute-force would equal to 2^(n-1). Mostly the real number of brute-force iterations will always be higher, but it can also be lower if the password is e.g. in a dictionary.
The maximum bound for a brute- force attack will be the cardinality of the search space.

This starts from the premise that the entropy of written English has less than 1.1 bits per character

This most probably counts true for the whole English corpus, but not for single passwords in general.

An example: Let's take the password "myPassword". It has a length of 10 characters. If the attacker knows, that the password is in the [A-Za-z]{10} space, the maximum bound equals 52^10 brute-force combinations.
As per my calculation, the password above has an entropy of 31.2bit (binned character-wise, not bitwise, thus may be inaccurate). That means, the lower bound to brute- force that password would be 2^31.2 (since the smallest length needed to represent this password equals 31 bits), what is much lower than the expected number of brute-force guesses (52^10 / 2).

From the perspective of security analysis, every password generation scheme can be thought of as a book and a coin.
The book always starts by saying how many times to flip the coin. It will then tell what password you get from every possible sequence of flips. So for example, a really lazy 3 flip book might look something like this:

Alternatively, you might have a 3 flip book which picks a Snow White character.
Now, here's the important bit. You might have been told in the past that when an attacker wants to break your password they'll try aaa, then aab, aac, ... aaz, aba, abc, and so on. Computer Security experts don't actually believe that. Instead, they assume that the attacker has a copy of the same "book" that you used to make your password. The only thing they don't know is what happened when you flipped the coin. (This idea is known in cryptography as Kerckhoff's Principle).
So essentially the attacker who knows you have Snow White book guesses the coin gave HHH, and therefore that the password was "Doc". Then she guesses the coin gave HHT, and therefore the password was "Grumpy". Because she knows the chosen book, the password "Bashful" is just as bad a password as "e" would have been if you used the first scheme. The way to get a better password is to start with a bigger book which describes more coin flips (i.e. uses more bits of entropy).
Obviously nobody would actually print out these books. It's a metaphor for the process that people use to generate their password. The process of genuinely random letters or numbers requires approximately 6 coin flips per character, which means the 8 character "L4zDigX1" would be in a 48 coin flip book. The process of genuinely random (using dice or a computer) common English words requires approximately 12 coin flips per word. That is the five random word "SweetsSpeechesCollegeStanceUkulele" would be in a 60 coin flip book. Suppose my process isn't random words, but is instead grabbing a random sentence from Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice. Now the 5 word passphrase "Adieu to disappointment and spleen." would require a much smaller book with just 13 coin flips. But that requires a random sentence. If the process involves picking a famous sentence from the same, "She is tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me." is probably in the top 16 quotes from the book which gives it just 4 coin flips worth of randomness. That is, famous quote are more predictable than random quotes, which are more predictable than random arrangements of words, which are more predictable than random arrangements of letters.
Now to home in on your specific question. How should we evaluate the strength of a normal human creating an everyday passphrase? For dictionary words or Austen sentences we could just list them, but listing (and weighting, but I'm not going to go into that) sentences you would come up with is difficult. So one workaround is to ask about the sorts of sentences general English speaking humans come up with.
One possible estimate is to take a big pile of English text from a bunch of authors, like Wikipedia. Next, we compress it. The compression algorithm will automatically learn a bunch of facts. It might learn that the pair "qu" is much more common than "qw". It might learn specific words, like "would" and "myrrh". It might learn that the word "would" is much more common than the word "myrrh". It might even learn that certain multi-word phrases are common. Once it learns all that, it will create a code which allows it to convert back and forth between English text and some much denser code. It should be reasonably obvious that if the compressed version of Wikipedia plus your passphrase is 24 bits larger than the compressed version of Wikipedia without your passphrase, your passphrase has (at most) 24 bits of entropy.
So going back to the idea that the attacker knows the book and guesses the coin, you might imagine someone trying 000010001100110100111010 (guessed coin) decompresses (known book) to "The cat sat on the mat." and so on.
To be clear, that is a best case guess. The compression algorithm wouldn't understand grammar. As such, some of the decoding attempts may not be valid. Further, it won't understand meaning. As such, it probably won't realise that "My favorite pizza is margherita" is much more likely (and should be compressed smaller/guessed much sooner) than "My favourite pizza is Toyota". Finally, it doesn't know you. So if instead the "book" is created by a modern large language model trained on the whole internet and fine tuned on your personal blog, the same phrase might turn out to be a mere 21 bits. But as a reasonable rough upper bound, the compressed size can indicate how (in)secure a passphrase is.

Even if you could decrypt the file, there is a good chance that it will not lead you to any other files... and even if it did, that is probably not why your site keeps getting re-infected.  In most cases of reinfection, the hacker continues to use the same exploit he first used to get into your site; so, the first step to keeping a site from being reinfected is to close the gaps in your security that allowed the attack to be successful to begin with.
There are better ways to clean up a compromised WP site
If you can restore to an older version of your site that does not appear to be infected, then do that first.  This is a good way to make sure there is no content left embedded in your database that you don't want.
Next, you should run all available updates to your Theme, Plugins, and WP Core since lack of patching is what makes most WordPress hacks possible.  If you do not do this, then the vulnerability that first let the hacker in may still exist, and your site will typically just get hacked again, even after removing the entire infection.  Most reinfections are because you still have the original vulnerability, not because you failed to delete some file.
Next, you need to make sure the site has a good security plugin.  Not only will they help keep the site safe, but they include tools that will make what you are trying to do much easier.  I personally prefer WordFence if you are looking for something with a good free version, but Sucuri, All-In-One WP Security, Bulletproof, and Jetpack are also decent options. Install it with learning mode off because you do not want it auto whitelisting suspicious activity that is already happening.  One thing this plugin will do is specifically scan you site for files in places that they should not be and look for files that try to obfuscate their functionality.  This way, if you could not restore far enough back, or if the infection had a long dormancy period, you can still remove it.  Chances are what has infected you is already a known virus and can been cleanly removed, and if it is not known, obfuscation is suspicious enough on its own to get a file flagged making them easy to root out, even if you can not figure out how they all relate to one another.  This is much more reliable than decrypting the file and hoping it has pointers to other files.
Most Security Plugins will also track if the Theme and Plugins you are using have been depreciated or not updated in a long time.  If you see plugins that have not released any updates in a long time, then it is likely that these are where the vulnerabilities are.  Replace any depreciated plugins with alternative, reputable, supported plugins that do the same thing.
Also check your user accounts to make sure that the hacker has not created himself an Admin user account which he could use even after you bring the security up to spec to continue installing malware.
If the Theme itself is no longer supported, then a total rebuild of the site is recommended.
If you do all of these things and the virus keeps coming back, then the vulnerability is likely at the hosting level, and you should consider moving to a different hosting company.

Generally speaking, geoblocking like this doesn't really do much to increase your security. Even leaving aside the issues with IPs that can't be easily linked to any one country or IPv6, it's usually pretty trivial for an attacker to work around them, because it's not hard to get IP addresses within a specific country. Some if someone is targeting you, then geoblocking is unlikely to help.
However, what they are useful for is cutting down the noise from untargeted attacks. By blocking countries that you don't deal with (or ideally only allowing access from one you do), you'll significantly reduce the amount of low level attacks (port scans, untargeted exploits, dumb brute-forcing, etc) that's reaching your systems. And that has benefits of keeping your logs cleaner and reducing the number of IDS/IPS alerts you get - which makes it easier to spot the more serious activity that can otherwise be lost in the noise. So if geoblocking reduces the load on your blue team and allows to respond more effectively to actual threats, then that's a real benefit even if it doesn't directly prevent an attack.
But you also run the risk of causing support headaches when someone tries to connect from an IP that's not got proper geolocation data, or when they go on holiday - which is an argument against implementing it by default.

The authorization code is handed over to the client in the front-channel and thus known by the user and everyone knowing the URI with the code (browser addons, server logs).
Exchanging the code for an access token (and depending on the use case also a refresh token) is done in the back-channel and thus allows the client to fetch the tokens in the backend and hide the tokens from the user.
The extra step also allows the authorization server to identify the client before issuing the tokens via the client?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?ÃÂs credentials or via PKCE (defined by RFC 7636).
By ommitting the extra step with exchanging the code you basically throw a key over a wall and hope for the right person to catch it...

Preventing authorisation code leakage

If the authorization code is intercepted during transmission (e.g. via a malicious app or a network attack), the attacker would still need to execute the exchange process with the authorization server. In the case of confidential clients, this exchange requires a client secret; for public clients, the attacker would still need to exploit a valid redirect URI, which is typically protected by PKCE. Which leads me to the next reason:

Support for PKCE

Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) adds an additional layer of security by requiring the public client to include a code challenge during the initial authorization request and then a matching code verifier during the token exchange. This makes sure that the client that initiated the request is the same client completing the token exchange, essentially stopping code injection or interception attacks.
For more information, you can read Oauth?ÃÂÃÂ?ÃÂªÃÂ?ÃÂs official documentation on PKCE in Oauth2.

One version of this explanation can be seen here: https://www.oauth.com/oauth2-servers/redirect-uris/redirect-uris-native-apps/
Mobile (and desktop) applications can - and many do - register a URI scheme (like "http" or "ftp") that they handle. For example, Slack has slack: (scroll down to "Deep linking with slack://"), Instagram has instagram:, and Steam has steam:. The app name and URI scheme won't always match, and in some cases an app might register multiple schemes. Registering the URI scheme is usually done in the application manifest, metadata included with the app that the OS parses when the app gets installed.
Browsers can be directed to those links as a way to open the associated app, and pass data to it. When a navigation URI isn't one the browser natively knows how to handle, it passes it to the operating system's URI dispatcher (in Windows, this is the ShellExecute API family), which looks up which app is associated with the URI scheme. In the event that multiple apps are registered, the OS might ask the user to choose (Android does this, probably others too) and optionally specify to always use a particular app in the future. The OS then launches the app, passing the specified URI as a launch parameter (or, in the case of mobile apps, invoking the URI handler page/activity). The app then parses the URI, allowing it to extract arbitrary data from the text - anything from somebody's photo on Instagram, to an OAuth auth code.
So, to answer your question:
You want to write a mobile app that will use OAuth2 (with or without OIDC) correctly. You do the following:

At development time, you choose a URI scheme - hopefully a unique one, in this example I'll use exampleappname: - for the app, and specify it in the app's manifest.
Also at development time, you write a function that takes the URI the app was launched with, checks for a relevant path (e.g. /oauth/redirect), and extracts relevant parameters like the authorization code, state, etc. This function, upon being activated with such a URL, completes the authorization flow.
Before publication, you go to the authorization provider and create or modify your OAuth client such that the URI with the app's scheme (e.g. exampleappname:/oauth/redirect) is an allowed redirect URI, so that the authorization server will permit the redirect.
You adds a feature within the app's UI to log in or authorize access, which generates OAuth request parameters (e.g. state and code challenge) and packages them into a URL (e.g. https://authorization.server.com/oauth?response_type=code&client_id=<your client ID>&redirect_uri=exampleappname:/oauth/redirect&state=<random string>&code_challenge=<PKCE code challenge hash>&code_challenge_method=S256), remembering the ones that it needs later, then tells the OS to open that URL in the browser.
At this point, the OAuth flow is ready, and you publish the app. A user installs it (causing the OS to register the app for exampleappname: URIs), opens the app, and interacts with the feature from #4.
The device's default browser opens that URL, where presumably the authorization server will either recognize the user already or ask them to sign in, then ask them to approve access if the app requests any, and then (assuming the user approves it) redirect the browser to the specified redirect, which will be exampleappname:/oauth/redirect?code=<authorization code>&state=<the random string that was passed in earlier>
The browser doesn't know how to handle exampleappname: URIs, so it asks the OS to handle it. The OS checks which app is registered for that URI scheme, finds that your app is registered (step #5, based on the manifest data from step #1), and opens your app, passing the entire redirect URI in.
The handler function from step #2 parses the URI, extracting the code and state, verifies that the state is correct, and completes the OAuth flow (either calling back to the authorization server itself or possibly relaying through its own backend server). The app received back the access token, etc. from the authorization server, and sets it in the app for use.

I can think of a few different benefits:

It slows down the attack, as you have to wait for the reboot to complete.

Forcing a reboot will kill any running processes, which might protect user data (such as an unlocked KeePass database or any encrypted volumes that are mounted).

On some systems (like macOS or iOS, no idea if that exists in Windows), there is a higher security state ("Before first unlock") between boot and the first input of a (correct) password:

Some data is encrypted at rest or only available in the Secure Element and cannot be accessed until a (correct) password is entered (it is then used to get access to a key stored in the Secure Element, which in turns allows decryption of the data). This is especially true of any stored passwords, etc.
Touch ID or Face ID are not available
Content of notifications shown is more limited
I believe there are further restrictions on USB devices
...

A reboot will bring back the system to that state with no risk of any decrypted data still being in memory, since keys are not available.
Note that this helps so much for security that they now added an automatic reboot for a device in "after first unlock state" after 3 days of inactivity. That makes it much harder for people to bypass phone security mechanisms (including law enforcement, see here for instance).

Since the script needs the API key as plaintext, you cannot completely hide the key. At least the account which the script is running under will always have access to the key, so if that account is compromised, any protection falls apart.
What you can do, however, is create a service account just for the script, ensure that only this account has access to the key, and that the key is encrypted at rest. I'm no Windows expert, but you should be able to access the Windows Credential Manager from the PowerShell. Create an extra service account for the script and store the API key as a credential for that account. Websites cannot read arbitrary cookies stored in the browser. This would be a major security breach, because cookies often contain very sensitive data like session IDs which can potentially be used to hijack a session. For example, if you're logged in at the website of your bank, you absolutely do not want the browser to share the session cookie with any other website.
Cookies are only shared between domains of the same site, i.e., a registrable domain like example.com and subdomains like foo.example.com and bar.foo.example.com. This is done by setting the Domain attribute of the cookie. Each domain can set cookies for itself or any parent domains within the same site. The cookie is then shared between the specified domain and all subdomains.
What a web application can do is send the data stored in its own cookies to a different site by triggering a cross-site request (using JavaScript, for example). This may seem like cookies are shared, but in reality, it's a one-way transmission of data.

A browser only sends cookies along with requests to the site that set them.  A web page, can have parts of itself that are served from different domains, though.  So a single web page can make many requests to different domains, each having it's own set of cookies, and each having the web page's origin as referrer.  Some browsers have been keeping the "3rd party" cookies (the bits and pieces inside the web page that are served from outside domains) in separate containers. Firefox for example: https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/firefox-rolls-out-total-cookie-protection-by-default-to-all-users-worldwide/  This would only send cookies to the 3rd party that were set in the web page host (1st party domain) + 3rd party domain context.  It's a two-site "jar".  So it stops the tracking chain that tracks the browser purely using 3rd party cookies.  It's worth noting that the embedded site can still know what sites you visit and tie in to you specifically if you have a login with that site (for instance a Facebook share button, or other 3rd party type login like a Google account)

To expand a bit on the blog post in browsermator's answer -- which I had to read several times before I could work out what was different from how cookies always worked, so it could have been written better:
In the classic cookie model, say that there's Site A (which serves ads or provides analytics or similar), and site B & C which use site A's ads.  The sites are otherwise completely independent (different domains).
You happen to visit site B first.  This stores some cookies for site B, and has an embedded iframe or img or similar for site A to serve the ad/analytics.  The browser allows site A to store its own cookie.  Site B's cookies are never visible to site A, but site A can see that it was loaded from site B (and can record that), and site B could choose to share additional data with site A if it wants to.  Since this was your first visit to either site, site A would typically just create a new random user id and record "user X visited site B".
You next visit site C, which has a similar embed.  Again, site C can store its own cookies, and when site A's embed loads it can't see any of site B or C's cookies, but it can see the cookie that site A stored when you last visited site B, which means it can now record that user X visited both site B and site C.
As you visit more and more sites that happen to also use site A's embed, site A is able to build up a profile of all those sites you visit, what pages you were on, and anything else those sites voluntarily shared (which usually won't be their own cookies, but could be other info they know about you).

What Firefox was announcing in that blog post is that instead of site A getting the same cookie jar regardless of whether you're visiting from site B or site C, they now get separate jars based on where you came from.  This still means that site A can track info about you from both sites (and can track you just as much as before within each site separately), but since each was a "first visit" they'll have different user ids and they might not be completely certain that both of them were you -- although there are other factors they can use to link the data, so it's likely not going to make much difference to data privacy in the end (though it's still an improvement).
There are some possible downsides to separate cookie jars as well, of course -- sometimes you want to have a common login shared across different sites, and this makes that harder.  But in general the benefits usually outweigh the negatives.

The individual exported private keys are the same every time. What you're seeing as output is a collection of OpenPGP packets, including Secret Key Packtets and Secret Subkey Packets which contain the encrypted private keys. Encryption is randomized at multiple levels: When GPG derives the encryption key from your passphrase, it uses a random salt to make brute-force attacks more difficult. And when the private key is symmetrically encrypted with the derived key, then GPG uses a random initialization vector. So the output is supposed to be different. When you import the private key, you'll see it's always the same.
You can inspect the exact OpenPGP packets with
gpg --list-packets /path/to/exported/data

In the secret key packet, you'll see a salt and a protect IV (the initialization vector) which change on each export.
The output of exporting a public key doesn't change, because there's no encryption and no other random parameters.

IMHO what you describe are different and mostly non-overlapping use cases.
What you describe as key ids are usually directly derived shorter representations of a key/certificate, typically using some (shortened) hash and then some encoding (hex, base64, ...) but could also be encoded another way. These are used to quickly identify a specific key or compare it with a given one (like SSH fingerprint on first connect, public key fingerprint in pinning, ...).
Key aliases are instead manually associated with a key to reference it later. While the term "alias" is common for key stores having a file name for a certificate/key is basically the same. Contrary to key ids such aliases are not usable for key comparison since they could stay the same even if the key has changed.
But, at the end "identifier" (as in key id) is a vague term which just says that it is something which identifies the key, no matter if directly derived from the key or manually assigned. Thus it might be used in both contexts. For example in JWK the kid (key id) can refer to an assigned name but could also be a derived id, it's implementation dependent.

Queues are essentially creating data at rest until the queue is consumed. I would expect more than transport level security, such as message based encryption or an encrypted blob. Also it's possible for data to linger in queues so there needs to be a mechanism or setting to enforce the removal of queue data after it is consumed, or some kind of cleanup process. Also check with your vuln vendor to see if they support Kafka/MQ/RabbitMQ. These products may have spotty coverage.
Note that MQ products aren't particularly better at "batch" or volume data. They are useful for loosely coupling business processes by handing off data from one point to another, presumable to be acted on later.
