Unproven assumption
There is one big assumption in the question (and all its examples): The apps actually have the data available to them.
This might not be true.
I can only speculate, but the following seems reasonable:
Signal
Signal is a communication app that delivers messages from one sender device to one or more receiver devices (and possibly other devices of the sender).
Signal might not store the messages on their servers (once delivered to all respective devices). Instead, all messages are saved locally for each device.
So when you set up a new device, they are simply unable to send you a history of past messages themselves. Short of instructing your other devices remotely to send your new device their locally saved message histories, that is.
Yes, you can manually go into the app and copy-paste messages from there, but Signal cannot do so from their end (or your new device).
Could Signal provide a button on your old device to export that devices message history? Probably. But that would require additional work: making the export secure (encryption?), preparing a way to merge message on import (if the same messages have been received on the target device in another fashion), ensuring secure transfer to the new device, ...
DuckDuckGo browser
The DuckDuckGo browser is a privacy-focused browser that tries to minimize leaking private data.
Part of this private data might be which sites you visited, and more importantly when, and what they (or at least their title) looked like at that point in time.
That would be the minimum I would expect from a "browsing History". If any part was missing, I think the value would be greatly diminished.
However, from a privacy perspective, each individual part can problematic.
It seems as a compromise for usability, DuckDuckGo only saves a list of sites you visited, not a full browsing history's worth of information. Likely that is why it doesn't provide you with one.

Side note: Although infeasible for this specific example, there are also datastructures that make extracting data hard or impossible, but allow specific queries over them (e.g. bloom filters).

Security, functionality and usability
In general, when designing apps, tradeoffs have to be made.

One can make an easy to use app that is completely insecure.
One can also make a very secure app that is almost impossible to use.
One can make an app with no functionality that is trivially secure and easy to use.
It it very hard to impossible to write an app that can do all three.

So choices have to be made. Different app developers choose different tradeoffs, but everyone has to make some.
Conclusion
These apps might not lie to you, they sincerely might not have the data you want. They are designed in a way that they don't need this information (likely stemming from a security/privacy concern), so they are unable to provide you with access.

The knoppix-data.aes file is created by the flash-knoppix script with the following command (slightly modified for readability).
cryptsetup create --key-size 256 --key-file - --cipher aes some-identifier /path/to/knoppix-data.aes

This command is equivalent to cryptsetup open --type plain in modern cryptsetup. So Knoppix uses dm-crypt in plain mode (at least in the latest version).
Plain mode works as follows:

The passphrase is hashed to produce the key, using SHA-256 by default. This doesn't involve any salt or iterations like in PBKDF2, so a brute-force attack is feasible given a relatively weak passphrase.
All data is split into sectors which are 512 bytes long by default.
There are different ciphers, cipher modes and algorithms for generating initialization vectors (IV). The cipher in Knoppix is aes, the mode and IV algorithms use the defaults. At least on my machine, those are xts and plain64. The first stands for the XTS mode, and the second means that ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂthe initial vector is the 64-bit little-endian version of the sector number, padded with zeros if necessaryÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ.
Each sector is then encrypted using the selected cipher, cipher mode and IV algorithm.

I'm not aware of any tool which brute-forces dm-crypt in plain mode. One option would be to implement it yourself. If efficiency isn't a concern, then you could also use cryptsetup itself: Automatically iterate over possible passwords, open the knoppix-data.aes file with them and then use blkid to test if the filesystem can be recognized (as suggested by TooTea). If this succeeds, the passphrase is correct, otherwise it's wrong (with a high probability):
# open file with a passphrase you want to check
echo -n 'passphrase to test' | cryptsetup create --key-size 256 --key-file - --cipher aes knoppix-data /path/to/knoppix-data.aes
# use blkid to test if the filesystem can be recognized
# check the return value with an "if" statement

Based on your description an authenticated client can get everything it needs to decrypt the data by running some Javascript inside the browser. This also means that if your site is vulnerable to XSS then an attacker can do the same - since XSS is basically Javascript running inside the users browser in the context of your site and within the same authenticated session.
If you would store something at the client side which cannot be retrieved by XSS then you either need to be sure that your site is not vulnerable to XSS or that the necessary secrets are never exposed to the client. The latter means that all encryption/decryption is done by the server and not the client and that the client only stores server-encrypted data.
While using server-side encryption/decryption would protect the encrypted data it does not help if the clients needs access to the plain data. In this case it does not even matter if the attacker can use XSS to decrypt the data, since they could also use XSS to access the already decrypted data - no matter if decryption was done inside the client or the server.
In other words: the only way to be sure that an attacker gets no access to the sensitive data by XSS is to either prevent XSS or to not let the browser work with the sensitive data in the first place.

There are several strange design choices, and there seem to be no clear design goals in terms of what should be protected from whom under which circumstances.
First, it's odd that you encrypt the data client-side, but the server gets to choose the key and transmits it to the client. If the server is malicious or gets compromised, this immediately breaks confidentiality, because the server can always serve some JavaScript code which loads the random key and the ciphertext from local storage and sends everything to the server. Then the server can reconstruct the encryption key from the random key and decrypt the ciphertext. Even if the server is supposed to get the data when it generates the CV, it shouldn't be able to obtain the data at any time without confirmation from the user. Otherwise, it makes little sense to store the data on the client rather than the server.
XSS attacks are also a problem if the attacker is able to obtain the authentication code through JavaScript and use it to get the encryption key from the server, or if the user has already authenticated and made the server put the key into the JavaScript decryption module.
So the encryption doesn't help against common attacks. You'd have to come up with very special scenarios to show that it's useful at all.
The technical details also aren't great:

To derive keys from high-entropy input, you want a fast key derivation function (KDF) like HKDF, not a slow password-based KDF like PKBKDF2
A key should never be stored as plaintext in local storage. Instead, it should be kept as a non-extractable CryptoKey in the Indexed DB.
Sending keys from the client to the server (or vice versa) massively increases the risk of a leak, even if TLS is used to protect the network traffic. A key should generally not leave the machine where it's generated. There are exceptions, but those require a carefully designed protocol where the keys are properly wrapped.

To fix the problems, I think the first step is to clearly define the design goals and the attacker model.

The signature is not sufficient.
First, the CertificateVerify message with a signature over the handshake is only sent in case of certificate-based authentication. Otherwise, there is no signature, and the Finished message with a MAC over the handshake is necessary to authenticate the handshake.
But even if there already is a signature, the purpose of the MAC is to let each peer verify that the sender has the correct traffic secret, as explained in section 4.4.4 of RFC 8446. Since the MAC key is derived from the sender's traffic secret (see the table in section 4.4), a wrong secret will lead to a MAC mismatch.

No, a direct CHAR or VARCHAR comparison in PostgreSQL is not timing-safe.
PostgreSQL internally uses the memcmp function from the C standard library. At least in the GNU C Library (glibc), the function returns early as soon as it encounters a character that doesn't match ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ and it's hard to imagine any other implementation.
If you want a timing-safe comparison, you need to implement it yourself. You can, for example, iterate over all characters and compare them without returning early. Or you calculate a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) of both operands and compare those HMACs. Since an attacker cannot calculate the HMACs themself (unless they've compromised the key), timing differences don't reveal anything useful about the password hashes.
Note that there are other issues:

The crypt function and its algorithms are largely obsolete. Only bcrypt (called bf in pgcrypto) is still somewhat acceptable, but far stronger algorithms like Argon2 have been developed since 1999 (when bcrypt was first published).
When you hash passwords in the database system, this means you have to transmit the plaintext password first. This greatly increases the risk of accidentally leaking the password, e.g., through the query log or in transit.

It's much better to hash the password in the application. This also lets you use more modern hash algorithms (like Argon2) which aren't currently implemented in pgcrypto.

TL;DR: In my opinion there is no relevant error here to fix. Instead your question is based on a wrong understanding on how DMARC etc work and what they provide, i.e. you wrongly assume that successful DMARC prevents classification as Spam.
Some basics: For DMARC to be successful is is sufficient that either DKIM or (not and!) SPF is valid and aligned. For DKIM to be valid and aligned it is sufficient that at least one (not all!) DKIM signature is valid and aligned - the rest gets ignored. DKIM alignment means domain given in the signature (d=..) is matching the domain in the mail headers From-field (which might be different from SMTP MAIL FROM).
So the non-aligned DKIM signature for d=amazonses.com you show does not matter. It will simply be ignored since it does not align with the domain in the mails From-field (d=amazonses.com vs. From:...posewith.app). Relevant for DKIM alignment in DMARC is instead a signature with your custom domain. Such aligned signature exist as shown in the mail headers and is also shown as valid in your third image.
This means DMARC should pass because there is an aligned and valid DKIM signature.
But note that valid and aligned DKIM, SPF, DMARC is not a guarantee for a successful delivery. Spammers manage to also have valid records here if they use their own domain. DMARC+SPF+DKIM is only used to determine if the sender might be spoofed, not if the sender is trustworthy or if the content of the mail is wanted by the recipient. So DMARC is only used as on feature from many to determine if a mail should be classified as spam.

There are two issues when it comes to encrypting permanent cookies.
First, the browser cannot tell which cookie is used for which purpose. Both permanent and session cookies can contain critical data like session IDs or authentication tokens, and both may contain trivial data that isn't relevant for security at all. It's entirely up to the application to decide how cookies are used. So when the browser encrypts cookies, it's unclear whether this has any benefits. If only the session cookies are critical, then encrypting all permanent cookies doesn't help.
The second problem is key management. Of course the browser could just generate a random key and use it to encrypt all permanent cookies. But if the key itself isn't protected, this is pointless. There are several options for dealing with this, yet none of them is perfect.

The key could be derived from a browser-specific password (similar to how Firefox generates the key for its password manager). However, this would require the user to enter the password whenever they start the browser, even if they just want to visit a completely public site that has no critical cookies.
Some operating systems allow applications to derive keys from the password of the OS-level user account. For example, Windows has the Data Protection API. However, this doesn't help against attackers or malware running under the same user account, and it's limited to specific platforms.
There are also operating systems which support more fine-grained key management. For example, macOS has the Keychain which allows applications to store their secrets (including keys) and decide who should have access to them. But this is again a platform-specific feature.

This doesn't mean it's wrong to encrypt permanent cookies. And it's certainly not impossible (as Steffen Ullrich pointed out in the comments, recent versions of Chrome do encrypt cookies). But there are some limitations which may explain why this isn't a universally accepted feature. Firefox does not encrypt cookies, and I'm not aware of any plans for implementing this.

Security, functionality and usability
In general, when designing apps, tradeoffs have to be made.

One can make an easy to use app that is completely insecure.
One can also make a very secure app that is almost impossible to use.
One can make an app with no functionality that is trivially secure and easy to use.
It it very hard to impossible to write an app that can do all three.

So choices have to be made. Different app developers choose different tradeoffs, but everyone has to make some.
Conclusion
These apps might not lie to you, they sincerely might not have the data you want. They are designed in a way that they don't need this information (likely stemming from a security/privacy concern), so they are unable to provide you with access.

As one commenter has mentioned, if the data is sent over HTTPS, then it is encrypted from client to server. However, it is not encrypted on your server. You should probably learn some basics about how TLS works (TLS is effectively the "S" in "HTTPS") and what TLS protects. The upshot is that it protects data in transit from the clients to your server, but not on your server.

It depends on who you're trying to defend from.
If the audio is going to be broadcast to "all other clients", there might not be a reason to encrypt it when it's on the server. However, if there are separate lobbies where only a small group of friends would chat, then it might be worth it.
In the modern age, you would almost certainly be using HTTPS (there are certain features you won't be able to use otherwise). HTTPS will ensure that anybody listening on the wire between the player and your server cannot see the contents.
What's stopping a random player from listening in to all the conversations? If the answer is "nothing" -- i.e. all the players are in the same voice chat -- then there's not much to be gained from encryption: you use encryption to limit the range of people who have access to some information, and if "everyone" is supposed to have access, then there's no need to do it.
However, if there are separate lobbies, such that all players within one lobby can talk to each other but not between lobbies -- then encryption should be used to make sure that even if someone pwns your server (and can record everything that's sent to it), they wouldn't be able to record the voice chat. This is called "end-to-end encryption": the message is encrypted by the sender, and it doesn't get decrypted to plaintext until it reaches the receiver.
You would need to figure out a way for the different clients to agree on a shared secret, while the server (which we do not trust to not leak data) doesn't know what it is. A very popular protocol is Diffie-Hellman key exchange: this allows two people to generate a shared secret, while communicating over an insecure channel (this video explains how it works). Since you might want more than two people in a lobby, you would need to perform this across multiple parties: this Crypto.SE post has some ideas for how to do it.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂJWTÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ isnÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂt an authentication method, itÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂs a token format. It seems you're talking about the OAuth protocol which has the concept of access and refresh tokens. The JWT format can be used for access tokens, but this is irrelevant here. What matters is how the authentication protocol works.
The short answer to your question: You don't strictly need refresh tokens if the access tokens are sufficiently protected. Otherwise, it's highly recommended to use short-term access tokens in combination with refresh tokens.
In OAuth, access and refresh tokens are used as follows:

The client sends access tokens to the resource server for gaining access to a protected resource.
Refresh tokens are sent to authorization server to get new access tokens without having to ask the resource owner for permission again.

Naive OAuth implementations only perform minimal checks of the access tokens. Once they've been issued, they're usually valid until they expire. This means there's a significant risk that a stolen access token can be abused by an attacker to gain access to the protected resource. To deal with this problem, a common approach is to make the access tokens as short-lived as possible, so that they'll (hopefully) expire before the attacker can abuse them. Refresh tokens then allow the client to obtain new access tokens. Note that the authorization server is required to authenticate the client (if that's possible) before issuing new access tokens, or they're supposed to implement some other abuse detection mechanism.
However, instead of first making it easy to abuse access tokens and then reducing their lifetime to counter this, an obvious alternative is to use secure access tokens. For example, access tokens should be sender-constrainted. So instead of simply accepting the tokens from anybody, the resource server should check whether a request actually comes from the client which has originally obtained the token. This can be achieved with Certificate-Bound Access Tokens or Demonstrating Proof of Possession.
To summarize:

If you can protect the access tokens, they can be long-lived and don't have to constantly be refreshed. Of course you may still keep their lifetime relatively short and use refresh tokens to enforce additionally checks before issuing new access tokens.
If it's difficult to protect the access tokens, then making them short-lived is absolutely crucial. In this case, you pretty much need refresh tokens.

You are confusing several different concepts here. I'll try to help you sort them out.
Tokens, in the context of security (there are other contexts that have different meanings) are something an entity - usually a person or machine or program - receives from some authority, and proves their identity (authentication) and/or permissions (authorization). In the real world, this might be a badge you show to get into a building or ensure the cooperation of others, or a driver's license, or so on.
In the context of computer/information security, tokens are short strings strings of data that are generally generated by a server after initial authentication (using other credential types, like a password or a private key) and held by a client. The client then presents the token to the server to indicate that it has an ongoing authenticated session, rather than repeating the full authentication process each time. Just like with physical security, there are different types of infosec tokens.

Access tokens authorize you to access some resource / use some service, often without actually showing your identity at all (they are purely authorization, with authentication having been delegated elsewhere). Access tokens are often, though not always, short-lived. A physical example would be a temporary parking pass you get from a machine and put on your dashboard, a key-card for a hotel room, or a actual metal key.
Identity or ID tokens, by contrast, prove your identity such as your name or an ID number (authentication) and other facts about you (potentially things like email address, physical address, and/or age), but don't inherently grant access to anything. Another server - not the one that issued the ID token, but one that trusts it - might authorize access based on your ID, though, without needing you to log in. A physical equivalent is a student ID or state-issued non-driver ID; it doesn't specify that you're allowed to do anything in particular, just who you are and some facts about you. However, it might be trusted to let you drink at a bar (if you're of age) or enter a restricted building (if the system knows you currently are allowed), even though it wasn't issued by the bar (which only cares about your age) or the building (which has a list of authorized students but wouldn't permit just any student). In infosec, ID tokens - like access tokens - are often short-lived.
Refresh tokens are sometimes granted in parallel with access and/or ID tokens, especially if those tokens are short-lived. Rather than directly proving identity to somebody else or granting authorization to a resource, they are tied to your identity on the issuing server. They are used to automatically re-authenticate you to the server, as a way to get a new access token without needing to log in again. They are only meaningful to the server that issued them; if your access or ID token expires, you go back to the authorization or identity server, present the refresh token, and get new ones. They don't have many physical counterparts, but going back to the hotel key-card example, if you lose the key card before your stay ends, you can go to the front desk and show your ID (e.g. driver's license or passport), and they'll give you a new one. The difference from is that your ID is an ID token nor a refresh token (it wasn't issued by the hotel desk, and is meaningful outside the hotel) but it's serving a similar purpose of a long-lived token re-proving your identity to get yourself a new short-term access token.
Session tokens are a generic term for any token that is tied to an identity and usually used with the same server that granted it. On systems that don't delegate authentication or authorization to a third party (that is, they handle it themselves rather than using SSO), session tokens are a simple way to remember who the client is. On SSO providers (authorization or identity provider servers), refresh tokens are, de facto, session tokens. Session tokens may be short- or long-lived, and short-lived ones may or may not also come with refresh tokens.
There are also other kinds of tokens, such as anti-CSRF tokens (including the "state" parameter in OAuth), which prove you're the same entity who interacted with the service at an earlier point. For a physical example, a raffle ticket is also a kind of token; it doesn't prove anything about you except that you at some point claimed the ticket, but you need to present it if you're going to redeem a prize.

In addition to the purpose and use of tokens, they can also be distinguished in other ways. One of those is statefulness. A stateful token is one where the issuer tracks the token's existence and the current state of its validity. In most cases, the token's state is checked on every use before being accepted. This is common for session tokens, especially refresh tokens. It is uncommon for tokens that are checked by somebody (person or server) other than the issuer, which is usually the case for access and ID tokens. Those are instead usually stateless, meaning once they are issued, they are valid until they expire. They can't be revoked, at least not easily. However, they are self-verifying - usually by means of a cryptographic signature, which works as an anti-counterfeiting measure - so that third parties can trust them anyhow. In practice, such stateless tokens are usually short-lived. In software - where a token can be used many times a second - they are typically very short-lived indeed, single-digit minutes, and paired with a longer-lived refresh token. Stateless tokens, in addition to being used for third party services, are also sometimes used (even on same-server systems) to avoid needing to look up the token in the database on every request. However, stateful tokens are arguably more secure; secure cryptography is hard, and if the key is compromised an attacker can issue themselves arbitrary stateless tokens that will appear valid. By contrast, validating a stateful token is pretty simple: what does the database say?
Another way that tokens can be distinguished is format. Just like how physical tokens can be anything from notched metal keys to a printed paper slip to plastic badges to a stamp on your wrist, a digital token can be a string of random bits, a structured text format like JSON or XML, or potentially other things. JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) are one of the most common formats, and are structured as three base64-encoded parts - two containing JSON and one containing the signature - separated by the . character. However, there's nothing inherent to a JWT that determines what it's used for. JWTs support (and approximately all of them use some form of) digital signatures and timestamps, which lets them be self-verifying and self-expiring, so they are commonly used for stateless tokens, which are most commonly (but not exclusively) access or ID tokens. Session tokens (including refresh tokens) and anti-CSRF tokens are more commonly opaque random blobs, generated by secure (pseudo-)random number generators. These are usually shorter than JWTs and are in some ways more secure (mostly by virtue of being stateful, but the structural complexity of JWTs also sometimes leads to vulnerable implementations) but are usually slower to verify (and increase load on the database server).
Yet another way to distinguish tokens is how (or where) they are stored and presented. Any of the digital tokens mentioned so far, by use or format, could be stored and presented in a lot of different ways. Even within the context of HTTP(S) specifically, there are different options. HTTP Cookies are a common option with browser clients. Because the browser takes care of storing, sending, and even deleting the cookie, the client-side code doesn't have to worry about it. However, they're potentially abusable for CSRF attacks. HTTP Headers are another option for sending. Most commonly the Authorization header is used, with the string Bearer proceeding the token; these are commonly known as "bearer tokens". However, it's also possible to use other headers, typically custom ones (e.g. X-AuthToken). Since cookies are sent in the Cookie header, cookies are technically a special case of this (and can be sent by a non-browser client the same as any other header), but the browser automatically manages cookies. Finally, tokens can also be sent  other places, like the message body or even the URL (though that is less secure, as URLs are more often logged and/or visible). As for storage of tokens, browsers manage cookie storage automatically, for non-cookies in browsers you can put tokens in things like local or session storage, and for non-browser clients you can use anything from plain files to credential storage to just keeping them in RAM only.
To wrap it up, tokens are distinguished in a lot of ways, most of them orthogonal to one another. A JWT can be an access token or an ID token or a session token or various other things, and there are also other formats of token you could use for those. A JWT is probably stateless but doesn't strictly have to be (though if you're using stateful tokens, it makes less sense to use JWTs, unless you're storing the JWT as its own refresh token too). JWTs, like all other formats of token, can be sent in cookies or headers or bodies or other locations, and need to be stored and managed manually if they aren't in browser cookies but are not vulnerable to CSRF if they aren't in browser cookies (or something else that the client sends automatically).

You're misunderstanding the recommendations. This is not about authentication (i.e., verifying the correctness of a password), nor does it offer a way to avoid storing password verification data like a hash. It deals with encrypting data using a password-based key.
The two possible options are:

You derive a master key (MK) from the password and then use it directly to encrypt data. This is the simpler choice in the sense that nothing besides the password and the PBKDF parameters is required to perform cryptographic operations. However, if the password (and therefore the MK) changes, you have to decrypt and re-encrypt all data that has ever been encrypted with the MK.
Alternatively, you encrypt the data with Data Protection Keys (DPKs) and then encrypt those keys with the MK. The benefit is that if the MKs changes, only the DPKs have to be re-encrypted. There's no need to touch the encrypted data, because the DPKs stay the same. However, this option requires you to store the encrypted DPKs somewhere (e.g., next to the data).

Both choices are secure (which is why they're both recommended). In both cases, the plaintext keys can and should be only kept temporarily in memory. Once the keys are no longer necessary, they should be cleared.
The prefix check you refer to is just an optimization technique when you're dealing with a lot of data. It's obviously not very efficient to first decrypt all data and then check whether the password was even correct. So the NIST suggests first decrypting only a small portion that has a known value (like a couple of zeroes). If that already fails, then either the password is wrong, or the ciphertext has been corrupted. In both cases, the decryption can be aborted immediately.
Verifying a password is a separate issue. If you don't actually want to encrypt data, then you should use a specialized hash algorithm like Argon2. Deriving a key from the password an then checking whether that key successfully decrypts some ciphertext prefix isn't any more secure than a hash comparison. In fact, the prefix ciphertext effectively is the ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂhashÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ. So no matter what you do, you need some type of verification data to check the correctness of the password.
If you want to use the same password both for authentication and for data encryption, then it makes sense to run the password through a PBKDF (which Argon2 can also be used as) and derive two keys: One key is used to verify a message authentication code and immediately check whether the password is correct. The other key is used to encrypt the data or the DPK.

globs are fairly simple, regex can be significantly more complex. Unnecessary complexity is the enemy of security, i.e. it is more likely to get it wrong and more likely to pass a review even if it is wrong. Apart from that, a badly defined regex can cause serious performance problems - at least in case when a backtracking regex engine is used like in case of the common PCRE.
This complexity problem is even worse if the pattern is not specified by a developer but by an administrator when configuring a product. Non-developers have usually even less experience writing proper and secure regex.
And if a server side executed regex pattern is controlled by a potential attacker, then a deliberately bad regex can be used for denial of service - see ReDoS. This is also true if the regex was bad from start (i.e. bad by developer or administrator) and the attacker could feed unexpected data into the regex to trigger a large performance impact.
There are cases though where the simplicity of glob is not sufficient, so it is not as simple as replacing all use of regex with glob.

If it was the MD5 hash of the filename then you would be able to significantly reduce the keyspace that you were searching, based on some assumptions about likely filenames. For instance, you might guess that the filename is likely to be 1-10 characters, then a . and a common extension (doc, pdf, etc). This is essentially the same approach that we use when cracking password hashes - we assume people will use common inputs and structures (capital letter, some lowercase letters, number on the end) so try those first.
However, if it's an MD5 hash of the file then the same approach isn't practical. Because while you can probably guess something about the file structure (for instance, all JPEG files start with the same few bytes), there's a much larger amount of data that you can't guess anything about (potentially millions of bytes of data, compared to dozens in a password).
So unless they're very specific file formats that only have an extremely limited amount of variance (less than 128 bits), then you won't be quicker than an exhaustive brute-force.

The PIN is not restricted to 4 digits, at least not on any modern version of Windows 10 + Windows 11 I have tested. However, in order to unlock non-numerical characters, a checkbox located right below the PIN input has to be enabled during PIN setup ("Include letters and symbols"). This checkbox is often missed when setting up the PIN. Microsoft apparently prefers users to select short PINs and as such only allows numbers by default. The length is also configurable, with 4 being the usual minimum (this is configurable via registry/group policy).
It is important to understand here that a PIN in Windows Hello is not the same as a traditional password credential. Windows Hello stores authentication credentials (like your face, fingerprint-metadata, and the PIN) inside your system's Trusted Platform Module (TPM). The authentication code used runs inside this TPM, which is supposed to give a higher level of protection compared to traditional on-disk storage. Most importantly, the TPM is protected by a lockout mechanism: Too many failed attempts will cause the authentication to be - at least temporarily - rejected, limiting the number of attempts an attacker can make. Due to the TPM's persistent storage, this information can even survive reboots, meaning that an attacker cannot trivially reboot the machine to continue brute force attacks. The TPM is also designed to be only attackable online: You cannot figure out what the correct PIN is without talking to the TPM.
This is vastly different to a traditional password credential, which is stored (hashed) on your computer's hard drive. An attacker can technically brute force your password offline by reading your password hash from the hard drive. This allows the attacker to get as many attempts as they have computational power, while this is not possible in a TPM. This is likely why Microsoft encourages short, simple PINs: Their security model differs from a traditional password due to TPM storage and hence can "get away" with having much less entropy.

The reason of a time-of-click check is threefold: first, it takes some time for Microsoft's scanners to analyze the link. If it links to a PDF file, for example, it may be analyzed in a detonation chamber. A time-of-click check allows message delivery before analysis is complete. If you do click on a link before the check is done you will be directed to a "please wait" message.
Second, the time-of-click check enables protection for already delivered mail, when malicious content is reported later, or the destination content is changed after the first scan.
Finally, the click is logged for future mitigation. For example, if it is later determined a link goes to a phishing site, administrators can determine which users visited it and place restrictions on their accounts.

You are probably using CRS 4 and running it in Anomaly Scoring mode (which is the default). In this mode, rules are not directly blocking anything and all of them are set to pass (see SecDefaultAction in crs-setup.conf). Instead, rules are just adding score and blocking is done by a special blocking rule which is doing it based on score.
You can try to do what you want by modifying the score which is added by specific rules, so the final score is not high enough to block the request, but this is going to be a little tricky.
All of the rules you mentioned are PL1 rules so they are adding score into variable tx.inbound_anomaly_score_pl1. The amount of the score which is added is specified in crs-setup.conf using variable tx.critical_anomaly_score - default value is 5. You cannot directly change this score or cancel it's addition but you can add more score using setvar action. This should work:
SecRuleUpdateActionById 941100 "setvar:'tx.inbound_anomaly_score_pl1=-4.9'"
In final, rule adds 5 score and subtracts 4.9 so it's adding only 0.1 score which is not going to trigger any threshold.

Long-term sessions are more valuable than regular short-term sessions and must therefore be sufficiently protected. For example:

To generate the session ID, the application must use a cryptographically secure random number generator.
The session ID mustn't be stored as plaintext on the server. Instead, only their hash should be kept. This prevents attackers who have managed to compromise the server from stealing all active long-term session.

Asymmetric encryption works both ways. You can encrypt (or sign) your binary with a private key. This can then be decrypted with the public key, and this also assures it was published by someone who knew the private key, i.e. you.
Most systems already have a framework in place for signing and verifying binaries. E.g. SignTool.exe or CodeSign.

Since you want to ensure both the confidentiality and authenticity of the executable according to your comment, you can combine a signature with symmetric encryption. For example:

Sign the plaintext executable with your private key (using GPG, for example) and store the signature in a file.
Put both the executable and the signature file into an archive.
Encrypt the archive symmetrically, ideally using a modern authenticated encryption scheme like ChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM.

The symmetric encryption protects the confidentiality of the file. At the same time, the receiver can obtain the signature from the decrypted archive and use it to verify the authenticity of the executable.

It's not true that compromising the private key of the sender (Alice) allows an attacker to read the message, because the sender doesn't use their static keys for deriving the message key at all, only the ephemeral keys. To decrypt the message, the attacker needs the private key of the receiver (Bob).
In comparison, if both used static ECDH keys, then it would indeed be sufficient to compromise the private key of Alice or Bob.
So when using (EC)DH, there are really three options:

static keys for sender and receiver ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ no forward secrecy at all; compromising any of the two private keys is sufficient to read a recorded message
ephemeral keys for both sender and receiver ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ complete forward secrecy, because the private keys are deleted after the session
ephemeral key for the sender, static key for the receiver ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ partial forward secrecy; compromising the sender's private key doesn't reveal a recorded message, but obtaining the receiver's key does

As discussed at length in Open Source vs Closed Source Systems, you can't meaningfully say whether open source in general is more or less secure than closed source; and you also can't meaningfully lump all closed source UEFI implementations together.
The only way that this question can be meaningfully answered would be to carry out comparable vulnerability research on specific implementations and then compare the findings based on your threat model.

It appears that in FIPS mode, by default, sshd uses hardcoded values for the ciphers, instead of using the values from the crypto policy.
In RHEL 9, the back-end file generated by crypto policies is compatible with /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and can be included by adding the following line:
include /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/opensshserver.config

In RHEL 8, the back-ends file provides a CRYTPO_POLICY= variable, which is loaded from the systemd unit file, but apparently ignored in FIPS mode.
Thus, there may not be a solution for RHEL 8 (other than completely handcrafting the corresponding entries in sshd_config).

The data on the drive is encrypted. This means that without the key:

the plaintext data cannot be read,
no legible plaintext data can be written to the drive,
random garbage data can be written to the drive,
data can be removed (by overwriting it).

Whether the encryption key is available to the second drive depends on the BitLocker mode you use. If you need to enter a password or PIN when booting from the first drive, then the software on the second drive does not have access to it and cannot decrypt the first encrypted drive. If the key is stored in the TPM and Bitlocker is used in "transparent operation mode", it is possible that the software on the second drive can retrieve the key from the TPM and use that to decrypt the first drive.
If your threat model is spyware (as opposed to nation state intelligence agencies), using Bitlocker on one drive gives sufficient protection against spyware on another drive.
